#3021. Ravens news: Eric DeCosta gets mixed grades for Jacoby Brissett trade

Welcome back to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of the latest news and analysis about the Baltimore Ravens. In today's edition, we cover a weak trade market for some of the Ravens' veterans, grades for Eric DeCosta's acquisition of Jacoby Brissett, and an assessment of first-year offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, Let's dive in:

Apologies to the Ravens fans hoping to flip some of the team's highly-paid, underperforming veterans for draft picks at the deadline. If Baltimore is holding out any hope of getting Lamar Jackson back, they will not trade away his left tackle, and neither Andrews nor Humphrey can be seen as upgrades right now. All three were listed under "no real market" in Jeff Zrebiec's recent trade deadline round-up.

One name remains: Roquan Smith. His contract seems untenable heading into the offseason, but another team could be interested in upgrading their linebacker corps this season. Getting rid of his future salary could help Baltimore's tight future cap picture and maybe even free up the money to re-sign Trenton Simpson. Some would even argue that a Simpson-Teddye Buchanan duo might actually be an improvement over Smith's up-and-down (mostly down) play this year.

But the Ravens love Smith. They loved him coming out of Georgia in 2018, and they loved him enough in Chicago to send a second-round pick to the Bears. And again, Jackson is still in the picture, albeit on the margins. With no clarity to be had before Tuesday's deadline, Smith seems likely to stay put.

It's worth noting that trading Smith might be less of an option in the offseason. Linebackers tend to have more value during the season when teams are desperate to make up for injuries and/or push all-in. But in the offseason, teams will have more (and cheaper) options at linebacker, allowing them to focus on premium positions instead. The same is true of running back. This might be the best time to trade Smith and Derrick Henry, but the Ravens will not pull the trigger.

It's hard to say whether there will be any interest in Smith. He's still an effective player, but he's 29 now, he's not making the same number of impact plays and he still has another year left on a big-money contract.

A purge of some veteran defensive players seems overdue, and moving on from Smith would save them $8 million in cap space, which would come in handy this offseason.

However, shipping off the team's vocal leader and defensive signal-caller could make it seem like the Ravens are waiving the white flag on the season. They probably wouldn't get much in return, either.

I'm mostly unmoved by this deal. Brissett does give first-year coach Jesse Minter and offensive coordinator Declan Doyle a higher floor on offense. Still, it's hard to see the Ravens contending in any meaningful capacity, especially with the disappointing way Minter's defense is playing. General manager Eric DeCosta gave up marginal draft capital, so it's a fine bet to try and salvage something from a season slipping away.

The Ravens lost 33-10 to the Jaguars on Thursday night with Fagnano (and also some Derrick Henry in the Wildcat) at quarterback. In all likelihood, Baltimore's season is over with Jackson currently on injured reserve and the team at 4-5. Ravens coach Jesse Minter has said Jackson's injury is "potentially" season-ending. But Brissett gives the team at least a sliver of hope of staying afloat long enough to hand the reins back to Jackson with a shot at the playoffs.

But make no mistake, those chances are extremely slim. Even knowing Brissett is about to take over at QB (and assuming Jackson has, say, a 30% chance of coming back in games starting in Week 14, ESPN's Football Power Index gives Baltimore only a 3% chance of reaching the playoffs. If Jackson is indeed able to come back, that number goes up, but it's still a long shot. The cost here is low. By ESPN's draft pick valuations, the swap works out to the equivalent of an early sixth-round pick. Considering the team's upside if it does get Jackson back, I think that is easily worth it for Baltimore.

Head Coach Jesse Minter gave a positive update Monday on All-Pro safety Kyle Hamilton, who left Thursday night's game against the Jacksonville Jaguars with a hip injury.

"I think everything looks fairly good," Minter said. "We'll find out as the guys come back in tomorrow (Tuesday). But I wouldn't expect that to be something where … hopefully he doesn't miss time."

Minter was also optimistic about cornerback Nate Wiggins (illness) and safety Jaylinn Hawkins (knee) returning to action this week. Wiggins did not play against the Jaguars, while Hawkins has missed the last three games.

"There's definitely optimism there," Minter said regarding Hawkins rejoining practice. "I think (Nate) will be okay. It was an unfortunate timing of an illness."

#3020. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday finalized changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements. The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.

#3014. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

#3003. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL). Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

In oil and gas, refiners and big energy stocks are generating cash for investors, and Morgan Stanley is optimistic more is coming.

The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF).

Fun Fact →  While nearly every other company calls Texas home, refiner PBF is headquartered in a suburban office park just off a highway in New Jersey.

Two big calls to quickly highlight in power production.

First, Truist says you have to buy First Solar (FSLR). The analyst upgrades it to Buy with a $270 target. Tariffs should help the Phoenix-based company, giving it pricing power for at least four more years. The Section 232 tariffs—which are too complicated to detail here—should help First Solar raise solar module prices and boost earnings. We agree, having written about the company and stock back in July.

Another call on the Power Insider radar: TD Cowen is starting coverage of TeraWulf (WULF) with a Buy rating and a $21 target. That indicates about 50% upside for the stock, but it's actually one of the Street's lower price targets. TeraWulf and other AI power companies have seen their stocks hit hard following months of big gains, but Cowen analyst Michael Elias says the valuation is now attractive and a likely lease in the second half of 2027 at a Kentucky location could be a catalyst.

In the wake of the terror attacks on Saudi Arabia, we spoke with RBC Capital Markets' Helima Croft about the attacks, energy and more.

The entire energy world is watching Europe's natural gas storage levels. The question is whether the continent will have enough gas to make it safely through the winter. Power Insider wrote about the topic in the last issue.

The fact that JPMorgan highlights expected weather patterns should tell you how much temperature matters when it comes to gas storage. The early forecast calls for October and November to be average or slightly warmer than the 10-year average. The red line represents the 10-year average.

Europe has been largely "saved" by mild temperatures over the past few years. Natural gas storage levels are lower this year than in years past, so the thermometer will matter a lot when it comes to how well countries can, ahem, weather the winter. Random, but interesting.

#3000. What are the worst NFL trade deadline deals ever? These 7 top the list

Every team trading for a player ahead of the NFL trade deadline is trying to improve its roster. Not every team that makes such a move is successful.

The NFL has seen many midseason trades throughout its history. That's been especially true over the last decade, as the league's decision to move the trade deadline to its current spot after Week 9 has correlated with a higher volume of moves.

While most transactions ahead of the annual cut-off have ended up forgotten, only a few have gone down as all-timers – either for better or worse. Seven trades in particular have aged especially poorly. Many of them have come within the last decade as trade volume has increased.

Here are seven of the worst midseason trades in NFL history, including one widely considered among the worst in sports history:

NFL TRADE DEADLINE: Everything to know before cut-off, including date, time, potential targets

Week 3: Indianapolis Colts kicker Spencer Shrader (3) celebrates with long snapper Luke Rhodes (46) after Shrader kicked a 58-yard field goal against the Houston Texans at Lucas Oil Stadium. The Colts debuted their "Anvil Strike" uniform - featuring an unfamiliar gray uniform and glossy, metallic blue helmet with the familiar horseshoe logo in white. The Colts won, 19-17, for their first win of the season.

Week 3: Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (17) hands off to running back James Cook III against the Los Angeles Chargers at New Highmark Stadium. For the game, the Bills debuted their "Nickel City" alternate uniforms - the most striking element being the blue "Charge Helmet," adorned simply with an oversized cutout of the team's familiar logo. The Bills won the game, 24-16.

Week 2: Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford (9) hands the ball to running back Kyren Williams (23) during a 28-6 win on "Monday Night Football" against the New York Giants at SoFi Stadium. The Rams debuted their new "Classic Sol" uniforms, an homage to the team's look during its 1951 championship season.

Week 2: Arizona Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett (7) hands off to running back Jeremiyah Love against the Seattle Seahawks at State Farm Stadium. The Cardinals wore their desert-themed "Rivalries" uniforms in the 31-7 loss to the Seahawks. Arizona's "Rivalries" look was one of the best to debut in 2025.

Week 2: The Baltimore Ravens' Trey Hendrickson (91) reacts after a sack against the New Orleans Saints at M&T Bank Stadium. The Ravens wore their "White Noise" uniforms, just one of the team's new uniform combinations that will debut during the 2026 season. The Ravens lost the game, 24-17.

Week 2: New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson (5) celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Green Bay Packers at MetLife Stadium. The Jets debuted their "White Out" uniforms for their home opener, which ended in a 20-17 overtime loss.

Week 3: Indianapolis Colts kicker Spencer Shrader (3) celebrates with long snapper Luke Rhodes (46) after Shrader kicked a 58-yard field goal against the Houston Texans at Lucas Oil Stadium. The Colts debuted their "Anvil Strike" uniform - featuring an unfamiliar gray uniform and glossy, metallic blue helmet with the familiar horseshoe logo in white. The Colts won, 19-17, for their first win of the season.

Week 3: Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (17) hands off to running back James Cook III against the Los Angeles Chargers at New Highmark Stadium. For the game, the Bills debuted their "Nickel City" alternate uniforms - the most striking element being the blue "Charge Helmet," adorned simply with an oversized cutout of the team's familiar logo. The Bills won the game, 24-16.

Week 2: Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford (9) hands the ball to running back Kyren Williams (23) during a 28-6 win on "Monday Night Football" against the New York Giants at SoFi Stadium. The Rams debuted their new "Classic Sol" uniforms, an homage to the team's look during its 1951 championship season.

Week 2: Arizona Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett (7) hands off to running back Jeremiyah Love against the Seattle Seahawks at State Farm Stadium. The Cardinals wore their desert-themed "Rivalries" uniforms in the 31-7 loss to the Seahawks. Arizona's "Rivalries" look was one of the best to debut in 2025.

Week 2: The Baltimore Ravens' Trey Hendrickson (91) reacts after a sack against the New Orleans Saints at M&T Bank Stadium. The Ravens wore their "White Noise" uniforms, just one of the team's new uniform combinations that will debut during the 2026 season. The Ravens lost the game, 24-17.

Week 2: New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson (5) celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Green Bay Packers at MetLife Stadium. The Jets debuted their "White Out" uniforms for their home opener, which ended in a 20-17 overtime loss.

Spoiler alert: this is the first of three trades on this list to feature a former Panther underachieving with his new team.

As a first-round rookie in 2014, Benjamin made a strong impression with his 1,008 yards and nine touchdowns. He missed all of 2015 after tearing his ACL in training camp, then returned in 2016 to the tune of 941 more yards and seven more touchdowns.

Before the 2017 season, the Panthers exercised Benjamin's fifth-year option. He rewarded his team with another 1,000-yard season pace through eight games and going into the trade deadline. But in a fascinating move for the then-playoff-contending Panthers, who were 5-3 after Week 8, they traded Benjamin to Buffalo in a move that reportedly came together three minutes before the trade deadline.

Panthers officials explained it was to eliminate redundancy with the skill set of Devin Funchess, a 2015 second-rounder, and give the team more speed options. For the Bills, they got a big, downfield target for then-quarterback Tyrod Taylor after their 5-2 start inspired hope for an end to their 17-year playoff drought.

Benjamin never reached the heights he had in Carolina after heading to Buffalo. He tore his meniscus in his second game with the Bills and only played six games for the team in 2017. Benjamin caught 16 passes for 217 yards and a touchdown. He also had one, nine-yard catch in the playoffs.

Twelve games into his second season with the Bills, Benjamin had an NFL-low 37% catch rate: 23 catches on 62 targets. Buffalo released him on Dec. 4, 2018.

But the 2024 trade that sent Mingo to the Cowboys certainly has not gotten off to a good start. The Ole Miss product was a second-round pick by the Carolina Panthers in the 2023 NFL Draft and had a mediocre rookie season.

Despite having the second-most targets of any Carolina wideout (85), Mingo caught just about half (43), which was third-most on the team and barely ahead of running back Chuba Hubbard's 39 catches on 44 targets. His 51.8% catch percentage was the fifth-lowest among wideouts with at least 40 targets and the lowest among those with more than 65. Mingo also struggled with contested catches, creating separation on routes and generating yards after catch.

Mingo's 2024 season started worse, with an even lower catch rate (46.2%) on fewer targets (26) and still disappointing production (121 yards) through nine games. Yet Carolina managed to bundle their second-year wideout – who still hadn't recorded a touchdown in his career – with a seventh-round selection for a fourth-round pick at the 2024 deadline.

With the Cowboys in 2024, Mingo recorded five catches on 16 targets for 46 yards, and still no touchdowns.

Carolina used their fourth-round pick to select running back Trevor Etienne – who showed promise in limited touches as a rookie last year. Mingo began the 2025 season on injured reserve with a PCL sprain and saw five targets in six games. So far in 2026, Mingo has appeared in eight games, tallying three catches on eight targets for 30 yards.

The 2024 trade deadline did not age well for most of the season's buyers. Meanwhile, the Panthers came away as relative winners.

Where the Cowboys' trade for Mingo was bad for several reasons – it was an overpay, Dallas was 3-5 at the time and missed the playoffs, Mingo has never been a top contributor – at least the receiver is still with the team. Such is not the case for Johnson. He didn't even make it through his second month with Baltimore.

At first blush, the rich (Ravens) appeared to get richer with the trade. Carolina was 1-7 and in clear "sell" mode. Baltimore was 5-3, just had a 100-yard game from Rashod Bateman and a 100-yard game from Zay Flowers in back-to-back weeks. General manager Eric DeCosta still felt the team needed one more offensive weapon to take it over the top, and Johnson seemed like the fit.

The Ravens sent a fifth-round pick to the Panthers for Johnson and a sixth-rounder on Oct. 29, 2024, and by Dec. 29 that same year, Johnson was off the team. On Dec. 4, the team suspended the wideout for one game for conduct detrimental to the team – refusing to enter a game because he was cold. Johnson never played again for the Ravens – the team waived him on Dec. 20, one day before his scheduled return from a suspension.

Johnson appeared in one more game that year – for the Houston Texans, the team that claimed him off of waivers – but was waived by Houston before the playoffs and never played another NFL snap.

With the pick return, the Panthers selected tight end Mitchell Evans out of Notre Dame. To date, he has 29 catches for 298 yards and two touchdowns in his two NFL seasons.

Chase Claypool enjoyed two seasons of solid production with the Pittsburgh Steelers after the team made him its second-round pick in 2020. Across 2020 and 2021, the Notre Dame product had 121 catches for 1,733 yards and 11 touchdowns.

In his third season, Claypool's role in the Steelers' offense diminished slightly after the team selected receiver George Pickens in the second round of the 2022 draft.

After Week 8 of the 2022 season, the Chicago Bears were 3-5 after a loss to the Dallas Cowboys on the road. Seeking a boost for its passing offense, Chicago traded its 2023 second-round pick for Claypool, matching the Packers' offer for the Steelers wideout.

The British Columbia, Canada native never played a full season for the Bears. In seven games in 2022, he caught just 14 passes for 140 yards. The next year, Claypool played in just three games, tallying four receptions for 51 yards and his only Bears touchdown before expressing frustration about how the team was using him to the media. He never played another snap for the Bears before they traded him to Miami in Week 5.

Chicago went on to lose every game after trading for Claypool in 2022, and the second-round pick it gave up became the first pick on the second day of the 2023 draft. Pittsburgh drafted cornerback Joey Porter Jr. with the selection, and he went on to finish fifth in the Defensive Rookie of the Year voting.

NFL TRADE DEADLINE HISTORY: What are the best midseason deals ever? These 9 top the list

Trent Richardson tallied 950 yards and 11 touchdowns on the ground, 367 receiving yards, and one touchdown catch as a rookie in 2012. At the time, he seemed the lone bright spot in an otherwise brutal year for the Cleveland Browns. First-round quarterback and 28-year-old rookie Brandon Weeden had the fourth-worst passer rating in the NFL. Cleveland finished 5-11 and in last place in the AFC North.

So, when the Browns traded Richardson just two games into the 2013 season, it was a bit of a shock to the NFL world. The shock faded once the Indianapolis Colts got their hands on Richardson in his second year in exchange for a first-round pick.

By Week 12, in early December, Indianapolis had already demoted Richardson to a backup role after nine games, averaging fewer than three yards per carry and just two touchdowns.

The Alabama product was only slightly better in his first full year with the Colts in 2013, and the team waived him the following offseason. He never played another regular-season snap in the NFL.

Thanks to a solid second year from Colts quarterback Andrew Luck, the pick Indianapolis sent to Cleveland ended up in the back third of the first round. That year, the Browns traded up from that 26th pick to take another swing at a franchise quarterback: Johnny Manziel.

NFL TRADE DEADLINE CANDIDATES: Will the Jets spring another November surprise?

In 1973, a 33-year-old Hadl played in his first season with the Los Angeles Rams after 11 years with the San Diego Chargers. By the end of the year, the former Kansas Jayhawk earned a sixth Pro Bowl nod to go along with his first-team All-Pro honors (a career first) and second-place finish in MVP voting behind running back O.J. Simpson.

The following year, Hadl started the Rams' first five games before being benched in the fifth game in favor of James Harris, who became the first African-American quarterback to start an NFL playoff game later that year.

Seeing an opportunity to bring in a battle-tested veteran quarterback, the Green Bay Packers sent five draft picks (two first-round picks, two second-round picks, and a third-rounder) to Los Angeles in a midseason trade for Hadl in 1974. The deal only came about because a similar trade attempt for New Orleans Saints quarterback Archie Manning fell through.

Hadl was a disaster in Green Bay. During his one-and-a-half years with the Packers, he led the team to a 7-12 record while throwing just nine touchdowns to 29 interceptions.

Meanwhile, the Rams went on to win six straight NFC West division titles and made a Super Bowl appearance with the help of some of those draft picks. Both cornerbacks Monte Jackson and Pat Thomas, second-round picks for the Rams in 1975 and 1976, earned multiple Pro Bowl nods with Los Angeles.

The Minnesota Vikings' trade for Herschel Walker is among the worst trades in NFL history, midseason or otherwise. It even has its own Wikipedia page.

Walker had established himself as Dallas' best player by 1988, his third season as a pro.

The year before, the former Georgia Bulldog led the NFL with 1,606 yards from scrimmage on 269 touches and earned Pro Bowl and second-team All-Pro nods. In 1988, he rushed for 1,514 yards and five touchdowns and caught 53 passes for 505 receiving yards to put him at 2,019 scrimmage yards. It was enough for another Pro Bowl appearance, second-team All-Pro honors, fifth place in MVP voting, and a sixth-place finish for Offensive Player of the Year.

It was enough for a Vikings team fresh off two straight playoff appearances to make a blockbuster deal for the running back five weeks into the next year. In October 1989, Minnesota received Walker and three future draft picks for five players, three draft picks, and additional picks conditional on the Cowboys cutting those five players.

Ultimately, Dallas didn't play any of the players it acquired in the trade. As a result, the Cowboys got the Vikings' first- and second-round picks in 1990, 1991, and 1992, as well as Minnesota's sixth-round pick in 1990 and third-round pick in 1992.

The Cowboys eventually used those picks to make several additional trades, landing five other players, including running back Emmitt Smith and safety Darren Woodson, to build a roster that dominated the 1990s. Dallas won three Super Bowls between 1992 and 1995.

Meanwhile, Walker played just two full seasons for the Vikings and never exceeded 850 rushing yards in a season. Minnesota missed the playoffs in all but that first year, 1989, with its new running back.

For those of you DBB sickos who care, I'm officially a married man! We had a spooky wedding on Halloween night and spent the past week in Cabo San Lucas for our honeymoon. We had a great time celebrating over the past week and a half!

JB Bickerstaff decided to mix up the starting lineup by starting John Collins at center. Paul Reed moved to the bench, and Daniss Jenkins was inserted into the starting lineup. Detroit started small with Duncan Robinson at the 3 and Ausar Thompson at the 4.

It proved to be the right idea early, as Collins was the leading scorer for Detroit after the first quarter with nine points. The Wizards took a 32-31 lead heading into the second, behind 12 points from Trae Young and 11 from Anthony Davis.

Detroit struggled to have an answer defensively for AD, and this was another game where Detroit missed Jalen Duren's physicality and inside presence. Davis had 30 points and eight rebounds at the halfway point while only missing one of his 11 attempts. The Pistons put up 37 points in the quarter with five different players scoring more than seven points. Collins led the way with 15, Duncan had 14, and Cade had 11 as Detroit held a 68-58 lead.

The third quarter was all about Daniss Jenkins. Cade picked up his fifth foul halfway through the third, and DJ took the reins. He made Trae Young look like a traffic cone on defense as Jenkins went on to score 13 in the quarter. He consistently attacked Young, and Young never stood a chance. Detroit continued to extend their lead as they were up 103-87 heading into the fourth.

The fourth quarter was highlighted by two beautiful plays by Ebuka Okorie and Ausar Thompson.

First, watch Ausar find Okorie in transition as Okorie does his best Kyrie Irving impression:

Second, the Human Swiss Army knife blocks the 7-footer Alex Sarr on one end, then follows that up by directing traffic and finding an open DJ with a great bounce pass for a wide-open dunk:

The Pistons will continue to hope for a speedy recovery for Jalen Duren as they needed his inside physicality against Anthony Davis, who finished with 44 points and 13 rebounds while shooting 16-for-21 from the field. Detroit still managed to pull away with a 122-111 win behind three different players who scored 20+ points, despite none of them being Cade Cunningham.

John Collins, in his starting small-ball five role, led the way with 24 points and 10 rebounds, shooting 9-for-13 from the field. Both Daniss Jenkins and Duncan Robinson added 22 points each, and Jenkins led Detroit with eight assists. Your fun fact of the night: Robinson led the Pistons with seven free throw attempts. There has been a clear difference in his game this year as he looks to get to the line more often. Cunningham added 17 points and seven assists.

The Pistons improve to 7-3 on the season. Detroit's home-and-home matchup with the Wizards continues as the Pistons will travel to Washington for Round 2 on Thursday night.

#2997. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#2991. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%. See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

Another day, another hilarious antic by Lakers superstar Luka Dončić.

While the Lakers were leading the Hawks 51-32 with 6:34 left in the second quarter on Monday night's road game at State Farm Arena, Atlanta called a timeout, which forced Dončić to show off his dance moves.

Luka Dončić creates a viral moment with Walker Kessler in Monday's game against the Hawks. NBAE via Getty Images

As he started walking back towards the team's bench and was approaching Walker Kessler, the song "Y.M.C.A." by the Village People began playing off the speakers in the arena.

Walker Kessler misses Luka Dončić's dance moves. NBAE via Getty Images

Walker Kessler moving past a defender in Monday's game agianst the Hawks. AP Photo/Mike Stewart

#2988. Fantasy football Start ‘Em, Sit ‘Em: 16 players to start or sit in Week 10

The 2026 NFL season is rolling into Week 10, and fantasy football managers will have to deal with a critical bye week for four teams.

The Chicago Bears will not be in action in Week 10 as Caleb Williams and Co. get a midseason week off. As a result, top-tier producers like Williams, D'Andre Swift, Luther Burden III and Colston Loveland will be out of fantasy lineups, along with Chicago's defense, which has shaped into a top fantasy unit since the Jeffery Simmons trade.

Fantasy managers will also have to navigate byes for the Denver Broncos, Philadelphia Eagles and Tampa Bay Buccaneers, which will knock out a few high-quality running backs: Bucky Irving, Saquon Barkley and Jonah Coleman.

Those absences will leave fantasy managers searching for depth on the waiver wire and potential plug-and-play starters who can be elevated from their respective benches.

Who can you start and sit in fantasy football for Week 10 of the 2026 NFL season? USA TODAY Sports outlines eight players to start and eight to sit:

Jared Goff, Detroit Lions (vs. New England Patriots)

There may be temptation to sit Goff after he failed to throw a touchdown pass last week against the Dolphins, but he has a favorable Week 10 matchup against the Patriots. New England has allowed a league-high 2,256 passing yards to quarterbacks this season and just struggled to contain speed threats Christian Watson and Matthew Golden in Week 9. Goff should be able to hit some chunk plays with his talented receiving corps.

Matthew Stafford, Los Angeles Rams (at Arizona Cardinals)

Similar to Goff, Stafford has had a couple of quiet games in a row, posting just one passing touchdown in each of his last two outings. He should be better equipped for a big-time game against the Cardinals, who have allowed the second-most fantasy points per game (FPPG) to quarterbacks this season, and against whom Stafford has thrown multiple touchdowns in three consecutive games.

Audric Estime, New Orleans Saints (vs. Carolina Panthers)

Three teams have allowed at least 11 rushing touchdowns to running backs this season. The Panthers are one of them and they have surrendered at least one rushing touchdown in five consecutive games. Estime took over as the between-the-tackles leader for the Saints last week after Kendre Miller's release, so he can be trusted as a flex with touchdown upside – provided Travis Etienne Jr. remains out of the lineup.

Ollie Gordon II, Miami Dolphins (at Indianapolis Colts)

Gordon has cooled slightly after four consecutive games with a rushing touchdown, but he gets a nice matchup against the Colts in Week 10. Indianapolis has allowed the fourth-most FPPG to running backs this season and is one of four teams to allow 1,000 rushing yards this season.

Jameson Williams, Detroit Lions (vs. New England Patriots)

The Patriots just surrendered a combined 17 receptions, 335 receiving yards and two touchdowns to the speedy duo of Watson and Golden in Week 9. Williams should be well-positioned to use his speed to get deep against a New England defense that has allowed the most FPPG to receivers this season.

KC Concepcion, Cleveland Browns (vs. Houston Texans)

The Texans figure to pressure Deshaun Watson often in Week 10, just as they did Justin Herbert in Week 9, but Houston is still susceptible to allowing big plays to receivers. They just surrendered catches of 58 and 50 yards to Quentin Johnston and KeAndre Lambert-Smith respectively last week and have allowed the second-most FPPG to receivers this season. Concepcion could similarly rip off some chunk plays thanks to his speed and elusiveness.

Darren Waller, Carolina Panthers (vs. New Orleans Saints)

Waller hasn't been consistent this season, but he remains an imposing receiving threat, as he showed in Week 9, racking up eight catches for 90 yards and a touchdown against the Broncos. The 34-year-old gets another favorable matchup against a Saints defense that has allowed the sixth-most FPPG to TEs this year, so he should threaten to score again in Week 10.

Baltimore Ravens (vs. Los Angeles Chargers)

There are precious few defenses that can't be started against the Chargers. Herbert has been sacked 31 times in eight games this season and has thrown at least one interception across those contests, making Jesse Minter's stop unit a high-floor play.

Jordan Love, Green Bay Packers (vs. Minnesota Vikings)

Love has been one of the league's most consistent quarterbacks this season and threw for 387 yards and two touchdowns against the Vikings in Week 1. Still, trusting him against a Minnesota defense that ranks No. 1 overall in pressure rate, per the NFL's Next Gen Stats, and has surrendered the fewest FPPG to quarterbacks seems like a risky proposition.

Kirk Cousins, Las Vegas Raiders (vs. Seattle Seahawks)

Cousins came back to earth in Week 9 against the 49ers, throwing three interceptions and logging just one touchdown while struggling to consistently distribute the ball to his top playmakers. The Seahawks are allowing just one passing touchdown per game to quarterbacks this season, so Cousins has a low floor/ceiling combination in this matchup.

Tony Pollard, Tennessee Titans (vs. Jacksonville Jaguars)

Pollard posted 246 rushing yards and five rushing touchdowns across his two games leading into the Titans' bye, so it's hard to recommend sitting him. Still, the Jaguars are allowing just 89.3 rushing yards per game, fifth-best in the league, so the veteran's upside is limited in an unfavorable matchup.

Tyler Allgeier, Arizona Cardinals (vs. Los Angeles Rams)

Allgeier handled almost all of Arizona's running back work with Jeremiyah Love and Bam Knight out in Week 9, but he turned it into just 46 yards on 19 touches. Allgeier should continue to have a sizable workload in the Cardinals' backfield rotation, but he is too touchdown-dependent to trust against a Rams defense that has surrendered just three total touchdowns to the position.

Tank Dell, Houston Texans (at Cleveland Browns)

Dell posted four catches for 105 yards and a touchdown on a team-high nine targets and saw his snap share increase to 47.1% in the Texans' Week 9 win over the Chargers. Will he continue to get that type of snap split and target share? If so, he will become a weekly starter because of his deep playmaking capabilities. Still, we'll need more than a one-game sample size to trust him against a Browns defense that has been solid against receivers this season.

DK Metcalf, Pittsburgh Steelers (at Cincinnati Bengals)

The Steelers may have to throw a lot to beat the Bengals, but will that guarantee a big game for Metcalf? He has posted three or fewer catches in three of his last four outings and is catching a career-low 51.6% of his passes. That makes him hard to trust even in what could be a higher-scoring game.

Tucker Kraft, Green Bay Packers (vs. Minnesota Vikings)

Love has focused heavily on targeting Watson and Golden this season, leaving Kraft as the offense's tertiary option. He has still posted strong outings most weeks, but he will be hard-pressed to do that in Week 10 against a Vikings defense that has been far and away the best against tight ends this season.

New Orleans Saints (vs. Carolina Panthers)

Some may look at Bryce Young's recent numbers (14 sacks, four interceptions over his last three games) as a reason to back the Saints in this spot. However, Young just threw for 276 yards and three touchdowns against a strong Denver Broncos defense, so he could be in for a good outing against a porous Saints stop unit.

#2985. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#2981. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#2980. Stephen Curry tries on former teammate Jordan Poole's sunglasses

SAN FRANCISCO ― There's a reunion going on in the Bay Area as the Golden State Warriors prepared to host the New Orleans Pelicans in a regular-season meeting at Chase Center on Monday, Nov. 9.

Featured on the Pelicans roster is their reserve point guard Jordan Poole, who was drafted by the Warriors with the 28th overall pick in the 2019 NBA Draft. Poole helped the Warriors win a championship in 2022.

During pregame warmups, Poole – who rocked a pair of athletic shades – had briefly reunited with his former backcourt mate, Warriors star Stephen Curry. Poole just finished his shootaround and was headed back to the locker room when Curry was also warming up on the court.

The two completed their signature handshake from years ago when Poole stopped to greet Curry. Curry couldn't help but to notice Poole's cool shades.

He signals to try them and on as Poole takes them off his face and hands him to Curry to wear for himself. Curry, of course, took and did 3-point shot with them on.

MORE: Is the greatness of Warriors' Steph Curry being taken for granted?

Poole played four seasons with the Warriors from 2019 to 2023, during which he averaged 15.8 points, 3.4 assists and 2.6 rebounds per game across 266 total regular-season games. He became known for his microwave-like scoring off the bench as he worked up trust between his teammates. He excelled enough to run the backcourt alongside Curry as a starter during the 2021-22 season as Klay Thompson, then, recovered from a torn ACL.

Poole developed the nickname "Poole Party" for his 3-point shooting and the range he began to develop.

#2971. Luka Doncic nearly notches triple-double as he continues to dominate NBA

The Los Angeles Lakers star nearly notched a triple-double on Monday, Nov. 9 in his return from injury when he tallied 32 points, 10 assists and eight rebounds in a 124-114 win against the Atlanta Hawks.

Dončić missed one game with back tightness, a win over the Detroit Pistons on Sunday, Nov. 8, but he returned to the starting lineup on day later at State Farm Arena in Atlanta. Sandro Mamukelashvili contributed 23 points off the bench, and Walker Kessler added 21 points and 10 boards.

CJ McCollum led Atlanta with 21 points off the bench. Nickeil Alexander-Walker added 20 points.

The Hawks took an early 15-7 lead in the first quarter, but the Lakers took control from there and didn't trail the rest of the game.

Los Angeles snaps the Hawks' four-game winning streak. On Saturday, Nov. 7, Atlanta had a star of their own return from injury. Jalen Johnson had 30 points and bounced back from a hurt ankle to help his team come back from a 17-point deficit and notch a victory against the New Orleans Pelicans.

Dončić's last outing was a massive – a 53-point effort in a win over the Portland Trail Blazers on Friday, Nov. 6.

The six-time All-Star is averaging a league-high 39.3 points per game this season. He adds 7.9 assists per outing, which ranks seventh in the NBA, and 7.8 rebounds and is making an early case for MVP. Dončić also leads the league in field goals made per game (12.1), 3-pointers (5.5) and free throws (9.6), while 49.8% from the field, 40.7% from beyond the arc and 88.1% from the charity stripe.

This is his third season with the Lakers after a blockbuster trade with the Dallas Mavericks that also involved Anthony Davis.

#2966. Patriots injury analysis: The hits just keep coming

The New England Patriots suffered one of their worst losses in recent memory against the Green Bay Packers on Sunday. Not only were they beaten with a final score of 45-27, they also saw multiple players go down with injuries. While not all of those were equally serious, some are a definitive cause for concern.

After rewatching the game, let's go through what is an extensive list for a team that has struggled with injuries all year long.

S Brenden Schooler: Already nursing a hamstring issue entering the game, Schooler was limited to just four snaps against the Packers — all within the game's first five minutes. The final one came on a Mitch Wishnowsky punt in the first quarter, and did not see the team captain suffer any obvious injury while working his typical role as a gunner. His hamstring still prevented him form finishing the game.

CB Carlton Davis III: While teammate Christian Gonzalez broke up a fourth-down pass late in the second quarter, Carlton Davis came up limping after making a cut in coverage against Packers receiver Christian Watson. He remained down on one knee on the sideline, and eventually slowly made his way to the blue medical tent. Davis was later announced as questionable to return with a knee injury, and ultimately ruled out instead of reentering the contest.

LG Ben Brown: Getting spun around while sustaining a pass block in the late second quarter, Brown went down after the play and received medical attention on the field. He slowly walked off under his own power and was later announced as questionable to reenter the contest with a knee issue. He too never came back.

TE Cameron Latu: Latu remained on the ground after a kickoff return in the late third quarter; he was taken down from behind while holding his block for returner Corey Kiner. He eventually jogged off the field and returned for the next special teams opportunity three minutes of game time later. No injury was announced by the team.

RB Rhamondre Stevenson: Catching a short pass near the sideline with under four minutes to go in the third quarter, Stevenson attempted to get up as normal but ultimately hobbled and went back down. He received some assistance by the Patriots medical staff, but walked off under his own power and into the medical tent. He departed for the locker room shortly thereafter and was quickly ruled out for the remainder of the game because of a knee injury.

S Jaylen Reed: The Patriots' No. 3 safety took a brief trip to the blue medical tent in the late third quarter, but remained on the sidelines and reentered the contest shortly thereafter. As with Cameron Latu, no injury was announced for Reed either.

LT Will Campbell: Early in the fourth quarter, New England's starting left tackle went down after blitzing safety Evan Williams collided with him from behind. Dealing with a knee injury, he walked off with members of the Patriots training staff and into the blue medical tent. The Patriots announced him as questionable to return, and he finished the game on the sidelines.

QB Drake Maye: The Patriots' starting quarterback took a hard fall on a 10-yard sack with 10 minutes to go in the game. He was a bit slow to get up and eventually pulled from the game, although the decision to remove him had to do with the score at that point — 45-21 — as well as an overall attempt to preserve him rather than any effects from that particular play.

WR Kyle Williams: Williams came up limping after an incomplete target in the late fourth quarter (that ultimately did not count anyway due to a roughing-the-passer penalty). He was not on the field for the next two plays, but returned for the two-point conversion after a Corey Kiner touchdown run. The ball again came his way, was not completed, and he was shaken up: the second-year receiver took a hard fall while trying to reach for the overthrown pass. He returned for the game's final two snaps.

As if losing by 18 points wasn't bad enough, the already injury-plagued Patriots also took some more hits on Sunday. Not all of them appear to be of the major variety, but some certainly are.

Rhamondre Stevenson, for example, is reportedly set to miss some time due to a knee tendon injury. Ben Brown, meanwhile, won't be available for the team against the Detroit Lions in Germany on Sunday. The statuses of Carlton Davis and Brenden Schooler, who also were unable to finish the contest, remain to be determined — as will any other effects from the game.

It wasn't all bad news, though. Will Campbell, for example, said after the game that he could have returned had the score not been out of hand at that point.

Still, the Patriots will once again be forced to adapt. At running back, this means potentially being down the top two options this week versus the Lions. Besides Stevenson, TreVeyon Henderson has now missed back-to-back games because of an illness of undetermined origin. This means that Corey Kiner, Lan Larison and practice squad option Terrell Jennings would remain as the only available backs in Week 10.

Along the offensive line, meanwhile, the Patriots' turnover at guard is set to continue. With Brown out, the team will either reinsert Walter Rouse or veteran Greg Van Roten, whose window to return from injured reserve was opened last week.

The Patriots will hold their first practice of the week on Wednesday before taking an overnight flight to Munich. They will then hold a light session on Thursday followed by another regular practice on Friday. Kickoff against the Lions is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. ET on Sunday.

#2962. Luka Dončić makes sure Lakers rookie gets a moment to remember after major milestone

Luka Doncic had already stuffed the stat sheet Monday night, but the Los Angeles Lakers superstar wasn't finished dishing out assists.

His final one didn't even count in the box score.

Following the Lakers' 124-114 victory over the Atlanta Hawks, Doncic was spotted tracking down a referee to retrieve the game ball as players exchanged handshakes and pleasantries at the final buzzer.

Luka Doncic of the Los Angeles Lakers handles the ball against the Atlanta Hawks during an NBA game in Atlanta, Georgia, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

The reason? Lakers rookie Cameron Carr had just scored the first points of his NBA career, and Doncic wanted to make sure his young teammate had a souvenir to remember the moment.

It was a small gesture from one of basketball's biggest superstars, but one that spoke volumes about Doncic's leadership on this new-look Lakers team without LeBron James.

Luka Doncic (77) of the Los Angeles Lakers drives to the basket against the Atlanta Hawks on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, at State Farm Arena in Atlanta. NBAE via Getty Images

Cameron Carr (43) of the Los Angeles Lakers dunks against the Atlanta Hawks during a game at State Farm Arena in Atlanta, Nov. 9, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

With Austin Reaves sidelined on the second night of a back-to-back after erupting for 43 points Sunday in Detroit, Carr received seven minutes of playing time.

The rookie scored his first NBA basket on a breakaway dunk at the end of the first quarter, courtesy of an assist from Doncic, who apparently decided that helping Carr make history wasn't enough. He wanted to preserve it, too.

Doncic finished with a ridiculous 32 points, 10 assists, eight rebounds, five steals and two blocks, becoming one of only 10 players in NBA history to record multiple games with at least 30 points, five rebounds, five assists and five steals. This was Doncic's fifth such game of his career.

After the game, Doncic was asked about grabbing the game ball for Carr.

"Yeah obviously you know you always wanna remember your first bucket, you know? And you wanna get that ball so it was kind of important for me to grab it," said Doncic.

The victory improved Los Angeles to an NBA-best 10-2, its best start since the 2019-20 season, when the Lakers eventually captured their 17th NBA championship.
