#2958. The Good, The Bad and The Ugly in Bengals’ 34-17 win over Falcons in Madrid

¡Olé! The Cincinnati Bengals took their show to Madrid on Sunday, and the stripes looked right at home at the Bernabéu. Cincinnati spotted the Atlanta Falcons a touchdown on the opening drive, then took over behind Joe Burrow and Ja'Marr Chase on the way to a 34-17 win. It's the first victory in franchise history in a game played outside the United States.

That's four straight wins; the Bengals are 6-2, and Pittsburgh comes to Paycor for Sunday Night Football next week. Before we turn the page, let's break this one down.

Joe Burrow, MVP candidate. Burrow went 24-of-29 for 271 yards, three touchdowns, no turnovers, and a 140.1 passer rating, then added a 1-yard sneak for a fourth score. He was nearly perfect in the first half, at 16-of-18 for 234 yards and two touchdowns. His 21 touchdown passes lead the NFL, and he has 16 total touchdowns over the last four games. After last week's three interceptions, this was the clean, surgical Burrow we know.

Ja'Marr Chase, "best in the world." That's how Zac Taylor described him after the game, and it's hard to argue. Chase answered Atlanta's opening score with a 47-yard touchdown on the Bengals' first possession. He had eight catches for 142 yards in the first half alone, the most first-half receiving yards of his career, and finished with 10 catches for 155 yards. His seven receiving touchdowns lead the AFC.

Tee Higgins in the red zone. Higgins only had five catches for 32 yards, but two of them were touchdowns, from 4 and 8 yards out. That's six touchdown catches on the year, and four in the last two games.

A run game that showed up. For the first time this season, the ground game gave defenses something to think about. Chase Brown ran nine times for 57 yards and added three catches for 18 more, and the Bengals ran for 123 yards at 5.1 yards a carry. One week doesn't fix a season-long problem, but it's a start.

Evan McPherson's leg. McPherson drilled a 57-yarder right before halftime to make it 24-10 and added a 43-yarder in the fourth. He has now made 23 straight field goals, the longest streak in franchise history and the longest active streak in the NFL.

Taking care of the football. Zero turnovers, one week after four of them. Linebacker Barrett Carter also picked off Michael Penix Jr. in the fourth quarter for his first interception of the season.

History, twice. It's the Bengals' fourth straight game with 30 or more points, tying a franchise record, and their first win ever outside the U.S. Taylor called the turnout of Bengals fans in Spain "unbelievable."

The run defense, again. Atlanta ran for 157 yards on just 24 carries, a 6.5-yard average, and Bijan Robinson punched in a 1-yard touchdown in the third quarter. For the second straight week, an opponent ran wherever it wanted. Pittsburgh will have watched the tape.

No pass rush. The Bengals finished without a sack, and the box score credits them with zero quarterback hits. Penix was never forced into a rushed decision. Against better quarterbacks, a clean pocket all day gets you beat.

Getting off the field on third down. Long third downs have been a problem all season, and this game was no exception. On a third-and-13, Robinson took a screen past a missed tackle and moved the chains. That's a drive that should've ended.

The slow defensive start. The offense finally started fast, but the defense gave up a touchdown on Atlanta's opening drive. It's the third straight week the Bengals trailed early.

The back end units of the defense. This one's tough to watch from the back end of the defense's perspective. It will be interesting to see if this is a position that the Bengals explore for possible trade depth.

DJ Turner II was flagged twice for defensive pass interference covering Drake London, and both penalties set up Falcons touchdowns. He also missed the tackle that let Robinson convert that third-and-13 screen. Turner has had many good moments this year, but Sunday was one to forget.

The whole back end, including safeties and linebackers in coverage, struggled to rally and tackle in space. Bijan Robinson, including on that third-and-13 screen, finished with six catches for 47 yards on top of his 100 rushing yards. The safeties and linebackers kept letting Atlanta off the hook on third-and-long, a problem that has followed this defense all season. Jordan Battle had an opportunity at an interception after jumping a route, and let a game-sealing interception through his hands (Barrett Carter later atoned for that mistake).

To be fair, the raw passing numbers weren't bad. Michael Penix Jr. threw for just 162 yards, Kyle Pitts was held to three catches for 23 yards, and Drake London had five for 68. The problem is timing. The flags, missed tackles, and third-down breakdowns came at the worst moments and kept Falcons drives alive. Against the Steelers on Sunday night, those mistakes will cost points.

Free yards. An offside penalty turned an Atlanta punt into a field goal, and the defense let a late first-half Falcons drive stretch until just 57 seconds remained. Atlanta helped the Bengals out with 12 penalties for 88 yards of its own, plus a missed field goal. A sharper team won't be so generous.

The bottom line: when the offense scores 30-plus every week, the defense can survive days like this. Come January, it won't be enough.

What was your Good, Bad, and Ugly from Madrid? Is Burrow the MVP front-runner right now, and how worried are you about the run defense with the Steelers coming to town on Sunday night? Let me hear it in the comments.

#2955. Seven times Jamal Shead looked Kyle Lowry-esque in loss to Grizzlies

The Toronto Raptors may have fallen to the Memphis Grizzlies 118-102 on Monday, but there was a familiar presence on the court that both softened the blow of a loss and boosted hopes for the future.

With Kawhi Leonard, Scottie Barnes, Collin Murray-Boyles and especially Immanuel Quickley out with injury, it was a chance for Jamal Shead to step up. Shead ultimately did so while summoning the spirit of Kyle Lowry.

Here are seven examples of how Shead looked like the Raptors legend during the game:

One thing Lowry was known for – other than his ability to lull opponents into committing offensive fouls – was his uncanny feel for the game. Whatever the Raptors needed at any given moment, Lowry usually dug into his deep bag of tricks to supply it. When Toronto was a horrendous 0-for-6 from the perimeter, it was Shead who hit the team's first three of the game.

The point guard followed that up with two additional threes before the end of the first quarter. Shead's three triples were the only shots Toronto made from beyond-the-arc in the opening frame. Considering Shead entered the contest shooting a career-low 21.7 per cent from the perimeter, it was very "Lowry" of him to transform into a deadly shooter when the moment called for it.

"Me being aggressive is going to add fuel to us," said Shead. "They won't be able to load up on Scottie, load up on Kawhi, load up on IQ."

Shead finished with four three-pointers, the most he's made this season. It's the most threes Shead has made since Dec. 9, 2025 against the New York Knicks.

Speaking of lulling opponents into a false sense of security, a player can't have a Lowry-type game without drawing at least one offensive foul. In the second quarter, while Memphis was in semi-transition, Shead drew an offensive foul on Taylor Hendricks.

After the whistle was blown, and while Shead was on the ground, the point guard enthusiastically pointed the other way. It was easy for those in attendance at the Scotiabank Arena to cheer the blue-collar play. Even for those who don't ever see the sequence, if you've watched the Raptors before, you know exactly what this looked like.

Despite the outcome, it still ended up being one of Shead's best performances as a professional. Shead finished with 20 points on 35.2 per cent shooting. He was two points shy of tying his career-high (22 points vs. the Philadelphia 76ers on Jan. 11 in 2026).

The uptick in usage was obviously due to the Raptors' injuries, but Shead was ready for the call.

"A lot of guys wait for those opportunities and are just ready to play," said Shead. "Obviously those are really important pieces for us…but when they're out, it's just next-man up."

Authoring a career-type game while undermanned is very Lowry-coded.

Lowry's stature may have prevented him from living above the rim during his 20-year career, but it didn't stop him from controlling the painted area – and it didn't matter how much height he was giving up.

On two separate occasions, Grizzlies rookie Cameron Boozer had Shead pinned in the paint. The first example occurred in the opening quarter. Shead leaned his body into Boozer's back, daring Memphis to throw the entry pass. Instead, the Grizzlies opted out.

Later in the game, Boozer received a pass near the basket with Shead guarding him. While Shead's help lurked nearby, Boozer quickly passed to the opposite side instead of taking advantage of his size.

While Shead may be light-years away from reaching Lowry's all-time Raptors assists record – 3,447 to be exact – that shouldn't take away from the fact that he's an excellent table-setter. After setting a career-high in assists (16) against the Milwaukee Bucks on Nov. 6, Shead continued to show his playmaking chops against Memphis. He led Toronto in assists with 11.

It's also the way he got his teammates the ball that mirrored Lowry.

Shead's Nash dribble as he exited the baseline before throwing the lob pass was fun. Later in the game, Shead's dribble drive opened up the lanes and as soon as the Memphis defence committed, he kicked it to the corner for an Allen Graves three. Shead's paint touches and vision also make the game visibly easier for Jakob Poeltl.

"We had a lot of great conversations during the game about where he's going to be," said Shead. "He's very mobile and can kind of handle the ball. He's really smart…it's really easy playing with Jak."

An endless amount of pocket passes, dump-offs and alley-oops allowed Poeltl to have his best game of the season. Poeltl finished with 18 points and eight rebounds.

The only player that might've thrown a better outlet pass as a Raptor than Lowry was Marc Gasol, but Shead definitely added to his resume against the Grizzlies. In the second quarter, Shead corralled a defensive rebound and immediately threw a deep ball to Walter on the break. The play shifted the momentum and brought the entire Raptors bench, including Barnes, off their feet.

"Those guys really want to be out there," said Shead. "But they're really engaged with us regardless if they're out there or not, and that's really helpful."

Later in the fourth quarter, Shead fought through the trees and somehow snagged the defensive rebound. Without hesitation, he launched a perfect outlet pass to Jamison Battle in stride, subsequently leading to an easy two points during a pivotal moment in the game.

Lowry had a knack for coming up with clutch defensive plays, especially when the Raptors were in dire need of a stop. When Graves helped knock a ball loose at the top of the arc, Shead teleported to the ball and rushed down the court for a breakaway layup, sending the home crowd into a frenzy.

Moments later, while getting back on defence, Shead motioned to the bench to ask for a breather. Before the whistle blew, Shead swiped at the ball while Canadian Zach Edey had it under the basket, causing it to go off his leg and out of bounds. As the crowd roared, Shead yelled as he walked back to the bench. The play was ultimately overturned due to a Poeltl foul, but it highlighted just how much passion and bravado Shead brings to the team.

Even while taking on a larger responsibility on the offensive end, Shead is still finding ways to impact the game defensively, just like Lowry.

"The more minutes I've been playing, I've took off the gas a little bit on the defensive side," said Shead. "Once those guys come back, I get to do what I do best and go guard the ball."

#2954. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#2953. Hegseth impeachment articles introduced by Rep. Massie

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., on Monday introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, triggering a vote in the House of Representatives as early as this week.

The unusual impeachment push against Hegseth by a member of his own party comes after Democrats swept to majorities in both the House and Senate during last week's midterm elections. Many Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have cited the Iran war Hegseth has led as a reason for the electoral bludgeoning.

Massie, who lost his reelection bid in a Republican primary in May, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth. They include waging war in contravention of war powers resolutions Congress passed to limit war, extrajudicial killings tied to boat strikes in the Caribbean that purported to target drug smugglers and suppressing free speech by targeting Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a veteran.

"Wherefore, Secretary of Defense Peter Hegseth, by such conduct, has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law," the articles, which Massie read from the House floor, read. "Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States."

Massie's resolution will force House Republican leaders to put the measure up for a vote by the end of this week. Impeachment resolutions are privileged, meaning the House must act on them, table them or vote to refer them to committee within two legislative days.

President Donald Trump once again defended Hegseth later Monday, telling reporters at the White House he will stand by the secretary even if he is impeached.

"He won two wars. He was in charge," said Trump, who was impeached twice in his first presidential term.

Trump also credited Hegseth with boosting military recruitment, claiming there are "waiting lists of people trying to get in."

Congress has the authority to impeach Cabinet secretaries, though it is a highly unusual move. Republican leadership in the House has not yet laid out how they plan to deal with the Hegseth impeachment, and it is unclear whether they have the votes to dispose of Massie's measure following the election.

The last Cabinet Secretary to be impeached was Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024 over his handling of the U.S.-Mexico border. Before Mayorkas, a Cabinet secretary had not been impeached since Secretary of War William Belknap in 1876. Neither was convicted by the Senate.

If the House votes to impeach Hegseth, the Senate would be tasked with holding a trial and voting on removing the secretary from office. If convicted by a two-thirds majority of the Senate, Hegseth would be removed from office.

Republicans hold a razor-thin 218-214 majority in the House, meaning only a handful of Republican defections could result in Hegseth's impeachment.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., reiterated his support for impeaching Hegseth on Monday at his first press conference at the Capitol since last Tuesday's elections. "Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America's national security, and he's the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran," Jeffries said.

Hegseth has appeared to be preparing for an impeachment fight. The secretary put out a video last week defending his actions atop the Pentagon, and the department has led a media campaign to "Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic."

Hegseth on Monday announced he would hold a press conference Tuesday morning at the Pentagon. His most recent press conference way May 5, just over two months after the Iran war began.

#2952. NFL power rankings Week 10: How will trade deadline affect pecking order?

NFL power rankings entering Week 10 of the 2026 season (previous rank in parentheses):

[Editor's note: These rankings will be updated throughout Tuesday as deals ahead of the league's 4 p.m. trade deadline potentially change the landscape.]

1. San Francisco 49ers (1): If they wind up securing the NFC's No. 1 postseason seed, you can pretty much slot them into the NFC championship game. Including the playoffs and following Sunday's rout of the former Bay Area rival Raiders, the Niners are now 6-0 with an average margin of victory of 12.8 points coming off their past six bye weeks. Also? The last time DT DeForest Buckner was on the roster, San Francisco wound up in the Super Bowl ... and it only seems right that Kyle Shanahan and Co. should get at least one game at SoFi Stadium this season after their September trip to Australia denied them their annual visit.

2. Chicago Bears (2): If they're going to win games on nights when QB Caleb Williams throws four picks, whether or not they're his fault? Look out for these guys, especially with RB Kyle Monangai likely back on the other side of the bye week.

3. Buffalo Bills (6): The last three times they started 7-1, the Bills went to the Super Bowl in each instance.

4. Jacksonville Jaguars (4): As if they weren't already playing dominant football, now GM James Gladstone is furiously reloading his defense ahead of the trade deadline. The Super Bowl window is decidedly open here … just hard to say for how long given how much of their future the Jags are already mortgaging.

5. Denver Broncos (3): The transformation of the offense since Sean Payton resumed calling the plays has been truly unbelievable.

6. Detroit Lions (7): WR Amon-Ra St. Brown hasn't scored since September and only has two 100-yard receiving games this season. Think the German-American star might break out Sunday in Munich − especially given how the Pats secondary just got shredded?

7. Green Bay Packers (11): Just when it seems like it's all coming together − OLB Micah Parsons nearing his return, the running game nearing its return − RB Josh Jacobs is going back on the shelf for a group that's won six of seven. But if mad bomber Jordan Love keeps launching precision munitions, the rest may not matter.

8. Seattle Seahawks (9): Just when it seems like it's all coming together − the running game restored and the schedule seeming to ease − Seattle can't keep its quarterbacks healthy. But if the "Dark Side" D, which has allowed three points in two of the past three games, continues to dial in, the rest may not matter.

9. Kansas City Chiefs (10): It's easy to miss, but coordinator Steve Spagnuolo's defense is starting to find a groove − allowing more than 300 yards just once since the Week 5 bye and surrendering more than 20 points just once over the same period.

10. New England Patriots (5): No Patriots team had ever allowed 45 points at Gillette Stadium. No Patriots team had ever allowed 45 points at home … since 1970. And these guys are supposed to be known for their defense.

11. Minnesota Vikings (8): This ranking feels too generous. But here's hoping they don't waste one of the better defenses we've seen this century … while also hoping that unit doesn't wind up sparking a locker room uprising.

12. Los Angeles Rams (12): Who's their top wideout for however long Puka Nacua and Davante Adams are out? Try Konata Mumpfield … who has all of 11 catches this season.

13. Pittsburgh Steelers (13): First place in the AFC North will be on the line Sunday night in Cincinnati. And the defense has gotten increasingly stingy for a group riding a four-game heater. Should be a fun one.

14. Cincinnati Bengals (14): First place in the AFC North will be on the line Sunday night in Cincinnati. And the offense has gotten increasingly explosive for a group riding a four-game heater. Should be a fun one.

15. Cleveland Browns (16): While the Bengals and Steelers prepare to beat one another up, the Browns, regardless of who their QB1 is, need to take advantage of their upcoming stretch of games − none that will require them to leave Cleveland before Dec. 20.

16. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (17): Truly a shame that coach Todd Bowles didn't take the opportunity to channel Dennis Green after Sunday night's loss in Chicago. "The Bears are who we thought they were! That's why we took the damn field. Now if you want to crown them, then crown their ass! But they are who we thought they were! And we let 'em off the hook!"

17. Las Vegas Raiders (15): They've rushed for more than 100 yards twice this season and had a season-low 24 on Sunday. They've allowed fewer than 100 yards once this season and permitted 190 on Sunday. Not a conducive formula for success … or one to inject a rookie quarterback into.

18. Atlanta Falcons (18): Despite being a half-game out of first place, they took Jacksonville's Godfather offer, which included a second-round pick, for defensive captain Jessie Bates III on Monday morning. Maybe recently reinstated OLB James Pearce Jr. can offset Bates' departure, at least in terms of defensive impact.

19. New Orleans Saints (19): Is Audric Estime the guy to energize a 26th-ranked run game? Sunday's 72-yard effort was the second best of his three-year career − and came six days after the Saints brought him back via a successful waiver claim.

20. New York Giants (20): Is someone currently not on the roster the guy to energize an 18th-ranked run game? RB Devin Singletary carried 21 times for 31 yards Sunday at Philadelphia in a game the Giants won despite averaging 2.6 yards per rush.

21. Dallas Cowboys (25): They outgained the Colts by 237 yards in what was easily their best defensive performance of the season − yes, that's a very low bar − and still barely beat a team taking its roster down to the studs.

22. Houston Texans (26): Their 3-5 start has been anything but pretty. But the upcoming schedule very much suggests the Texans could be above .500 by the time December arrives.

23. Carolina Panthers (22): With two of their next three against divisional foes and no games against opponents with winning records for the rest of the month, it's time to get right.

24. Washington Commanders (21): With their next game on Thursday night in New York, is Dan Quinn again coaching for his job after the Commanders' latest end-of-game play-calling misadventure?

25. Baltimore Ravens (24): They sure could use Jacoby Brissett about now − and presumably will debut the recently acquired QB on Monday night against the winless Bolts. And not a moment too soon considering the Ravens have lost three consecutive games by at least 20 points for the first time in franchise history.

26. Arizona Cardinals (23): They sure could use Jacoby Brissett about now − but let him go to Baltimore days before Gardner Minshew II was lost for the season. The Cards might also (kinda) want Marvin Harrison Jr. back, too, after WR1 Michael Wilson suffered a season-ending neck injury.

27. Miami Dolphins (27): After a couple encouraging performances, the offense has tailed off significantly in recent weeks. A trip to Indianapolis could be a cure-all.

28. New York Jets (28): They might be able to get a first-round pick for Geno Smith … if they shop him as a linebacker.

29. Tennessee Titans (29): There's a very good chance this team will get outgained by 2,000 yards by the time this season is over.

30. Philadelphia Eagles (30): GM Howie Roseman is waving the white flag now that they're now on the verge of losing eight in a row. The last time that happened, in 2012, Andy Reid got fired. Watch your back, Sirianni.

31. Indianapolis Colts (31): As RB Jonathan Taylor wants to learn who he'll be playing for in Week 10, make a bid for rookie RB Seth McGowan in your fantasy league ... assuming he's still available.

32. Los Angeles Chargers (32): Albert Einstein did not, in fact, say, "The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results." However he would surely agree with the sentiment, unlike the Bolts' brain trust, apparently.

#2951. SoftBank swings to $7 billion loss after U.S. data center hit and Intel share decline

SoftBank reported a fiscal second-quarter net loss of 1.12 trillion yen ($7 billion) on Tuesday, as losses tied to U.S. AI data center equipment procurement and Intel share declines weighed on earnings.

The Japanese investment giant also recorded a 597.2 billion ($3.7 billion) yen loss in the six months ending on Sept. 30 due to changes in procurement plans for power generation equipment for AI data center projects in the U.S.

SoftBank said it had made advance investments to secure power generation equipment for its AI data center projects in the U.S. amid concerns over potential shortages and long procurement lead times. Power is increasingly becoming a key constraint for the AI data center buildout as power grids become overwhelmed with applications from large energy users like data centers.

Cumulative payments for power-generation equipment for U.S. AI data center projects, like the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Pike County, Ohio, totaled $9.48 billion as of the end of September.

"We made bridge investments in advance to secure power generation equipment in anticipation of shortage," a SoftBank executive said during the company's earnings call.

Here's how SoftBank fared in the fiscal second quarter:

Revenue rose 13.3% in the six months ended Sept. 30, supported by growth in telecommunications and AI computing businesses. The company said its SoftBank segment recorded higher sales across all businesses, while revenue at its AI computing segment increased.

The company's Vision Fund segment swung to a loss of 81.58 billion yen in the fiscal second quarter, compared with a profit of 2.38 trillion yen a year earlier. Vision Fund 1 recorded an investment loss of $20 million in the quarter, despite a $1.3 billion gain on ByteDance, as shares of publicly traded portfolio companies, including Coupang and Grab, declined.

The Vision Funds segment recorded investment gains of 85.45 billion yen, down sharply from 2.81 trillion yen in the year-earlier period. Vision Fund 2 posted investment gains of 89.26 billion yen, while Vision Fund 1 recorded a loss of 3.86 billion yen on its investments.

As of the end of September, SoftBank's cumulative investment in OpenAI stood at $54.6 billion, with a fair value of $99.6 billion and a cumulative investment gain of $45 billion, according to the company.

SoftBank said a potential increase in OpenAI's valuation following a new funding round had not yet been reflected in its results, pending an official announcement. The updated valuation could be reflected in the fiscal third quarter, potentially boosting its net asset value and improving its loan-to-value ratio, the company said.

"ChatGPT has been continuously a weapon of OpenAI, especially for consumers," the SoftBank esecutive said during the company's earnings call, highlighting the chatbot's growing user base.

Shares of the Japanese investment giant closed 13.9% higher on Tuesday. The gains came as Asian technology stocks, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, rose following an overnight rebound on Wall Street.

On its AI infrastructure investments, SoftBank highlighted a 20-year lease agreement with OpenAI for eight gigawatts of IT capacity at a data center project in Ohio.

Addressing concerns of water consumption at its planned data center in Texas, SoftBank said it was taking steps to reduce water use through a closed-loop, air-cooled system. The company also pointed to plans to hire and source locally.

Ahead of its earnings release, SoftBank Group announced on Monday plans with Grab and Malaysia's PETROS to commit a combined $1.85 billion in initial capital to develop AI infrastructure in Malaysia, with a long-term target of at least five gigawatts of AI computing capacity.

#2950. USMNT could lose head coach just months after signing extension

Manchester United have gotten off to the worst start in their Premier League history, and it looks like Michael Carrick is about to pay the price. The club is reportedly ready to fire its manager, with United sitting in the relegation zone after just one win in 10 league games.

And United's top choice to replace him could come as a big blow to American soccer fans. U.S. men's national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino is reportedly the favorite for the job, less than four months after signing a contract extension with U.S. Soccer.

Pochettino took over the USMNT in 2024 with the goal of leading the team on a deep run in the World Cup on home soil. Instead, the U.S. was eliminated in the Round of 16 by Belgium in a blowout loss.

That run also came with its share of controversy. Pochettino later admitted it was a "mistake" after FIFA overturned a suspension to Folarin Balogun ahead of the Belgium match, a decision that came after President Donald Trump said he had contacted FIFA president Gianni Infantino about it. He also didn't mince words about Christian Pulisic's struggles.

Still, U.S. Soccer stood by Pochettino after the tournament, and in August, it announced that he had signed a new deal that runs through the 2030 World Cup.

According to ESPN's Mark Ogden and Rob Dawson, United's leadership, including co-chairman Joel Glazer and minority owner Jim Ratcliffe, has been assessing Carrick's future. Sources told ESPN that there is "now acceptance that performances and results demand a change of manager."

Carrick took over as interim manager in January and led United to Champions League qualification, earning a two-year contract this summer. But the club has won just one of four games since giving him time to turn things around last month, leaving United one point off the bottom of the table.

Pochettino, who has interviewed for the United job three times before, is regarded as having "the Premier League experience and personality needed to drag United out of danger," per the report. The former Tottenham, Chelsea, and PSG manager also reportedly has a $10 million escape clause in his U.S. Soccer contract, which United would have to pay.

Eddie Howe, Julian Nagelsmann, and Kieran McKenna are also reportedly among the candidates. United's next match is against Liverpool at Anfield on Nov. 22.

Needless to say, U.S. Soccer will be watching this one closely.

#2949. 3 takeaways from the Mavericks’ thrilling 125-122 win over the Indiana Pacers

The Dallas Mavericks (7-4) survived a wild one Monday night, beating the Indiana Pacers (3-8) 125-122 in one of their most entertaining games of the season. Cooper Flagg was incredible, finishing with 43 points on 16-of-25 shooting, 10 rebounds, six assists, and three steals, while Kyrie Irving added 35 points on seven made 3-pointers. Pascal Siakam led Indiana with 29 points, nine rebounds and eight assists. Dallas trailed by 10 at halftime, but Flagg and Irving powered a second-half comeback and made enough plays late to escape with the win.

Dallas opened sluggishly and spent most of the first quarter trying to dig out of an early hole. Flagg was easily the Mavericks' best player, scoring nine points with five rebounds, two assists, and three steals while shooting 4-of-6. Kyrie started 1-for-4, Caleb Martin missed both shots, and Dallas shot only 40 percent from the field and 27.3 percent from three. Indiana, meanwhile, shot 55 percent from the field and 57.1 percent from three, with Siakam going perfect from the floor for nine points and Aaron Nesmith hitting both of his threes. Flagg's activity kept Dallas within reach, but Indiana was the sharper team and led 31-26 after one.

The Mavericks found more offense in the second quarter, but Siakam completely took over. Kyrie got going with three threes and reached 15 points, while Flagg continued to create as both a scorer and passer. Walter Clayton Jr. also gave Dallas good minutes, but the Mavericks couldn't string together enough stops to take control. Siakam finished the half with 26 points on 8-of-9 shooting and hit five of his six threes, repeatedly answering every Dallas run. Indiana shot 60 percent from the field and 56.3 percent from three in the half, while P.J. Washington struggled badly at 2-of-10 from the floor. Andrew Nembhard hit a turnaround jumper at the horn to send the Pacers into halftime up 66-56.

Dallas finally flipped the game in the third, and Flagg was the biggest reason why. He scored 14 points in the period, getting to his turnaround jumper, attacking the rim, and making better reads as the Mavericks steadily erased the deficit. Kyrie stayed hot with two more threes, while Washington finally found some rhythm with a tip-in and a three. Dallas also tightened up defensively, forcing turnovers and getting better activity from Clayton and Naji Marshall. Siakam cooled off significantly after torching Dallas in the first half, and Flagg kept pushing late with back-to-back finger rolls to cut the deficit to two. Dallas closed the quarter down just 93-90 after entering it trailing by 10.

The fourth quarter was an absolute blast. Dallas and Indiana traded tough shots, mistakes, and momentum swings to the finish, with Flagg and Kyrie carrying the Mavericks offensively whenever things started to fall apart. It was far from clean, with turnovers, unnecessary fouls, and several possessions that could have swung the game either way, but Dallas kept responding. Every time Indiana landed a punch, Flagg or Kyrie found another huge basket. The final minutes turned into a possession-by-possession fight, and the Mavericks finally made enough plays on both ends to survive 125-122. It was messy, stressful, and probably harder than it needed to be, but it was also one of the most fun wins of the season.

Right now, the Mavericks need to do everything they can to keep Kyrie Irving in rhythm. Kyrie was great again Monday, finishing with 35 points on 11-of-18 shooting while hitting seven of his 10 threes, and it felt like a continuation of everything he started against Brooklyn the night before. Since returning from injury, Kyrie has looked noticeably better when he has been able to stack games together. He came back a little rusty, started finding his rhythm, then sat against Sacramento and looked rusty again when he returned. Now he has played on consecutive nights, and suddenly he looks completely comfortable.

Against Indiana, he was the driving force behind Dallas staying alive long enough to make its second-half run. Every time the offense stalled, Kyrie created something, whether it was a pull-up, a three or a tough finish around the rim. He had 25 points by the end of the third quarter and kept making huge shots as Dallas erased a 10-point halftime deficit. The Mavericks obviously have to be smart with him after the injury, but there is also something to be said for letting Kyrie play when he is rolling. Right now, he has his rhythm back, and Dallas looks completely different because of it.

Somehow, Cooper Flagg keeps finding another level.

Flagg finished with 43 points, 10 rebounds, six assists, and three steals while shooting 16-of-25 from the field, 3-of-6 from three, and a perfect 8-of-8 at the line. He was Dallas' best player early when almost nobody else had anything going, then became the centerpiece of the comeback after halftime. He scored 14 points in the third quarter alone, repeatedly getting to his turnaround jumper and the rim, and he continued making huge plays when the game tightened in the fourth.

What continues to stand out is how comfortable he looks with the game on the line. Flagg does not shy away from the moment or wait for someone else to create. He wants the ball, attacks mismatches, and has already developed an incredible ability to create something when possessions break down. His case for Clutch Player of the Year is only getting stronger because this keeps happening. Dallas needed nearly all 43 of his points Monday, and when the Mavericks needed someone to will them across the finish line, Flagg was right there again.

This is becoming one of the biggest differences between this Mavericks team and what we watched last season.

Monday was exactly the type of game Dallas would have found a way to lose a year ago. The Mavericks were down double digits, had stretches filled with turnovers, missed free throws, and unnecessary fouls, and gave Indiana plenty of opportunities to take control. Instead of folding, they kept answering. Kyrie and Flagg made difficult shots, the defense made timely stops, and Dallas stayed composed enough to survive a genuinely chaotic finish.

Close games are rarely clean, and Monday certainly was not. The Pacers shot 52.4 percent from the field and 42.9 percent from three; Siakam was incredible, and Indiana kept finding ways to punch back. Still, Dallas found a way to win 125-122. This team has the talent to make tough shots late with Flagg and Kyrie, but it also feels like Dusty May has given them more structure and confidence in those moments.

Mistakes and ugly possessions will still happen, but the Mavericks no longer seem to panic when games get tight. They believe they can close, and with Flagg and Kyrie playing like this, there is a pretty good reason for that confidence.

#2948. Greg Rousseau: Bills defense showing "what we can do" over last two weeks

The Bills gave up at least 29 points in five of their first six games of the season and opponents averaged over 386 yards of offense in those contests.

Concern about those numbers was mitigated by the team's 5-1 record, but it lingered as a reason to doubt that the Bills would be able to go the distance come the postseason. The Bills had a bye in Week 7 and the last two weeks have seen very different performances.

The Bills allowed 144 yards in a 36-10 win over the Ravens in Week 8 and they allowed 178 in Monday night's 23-6 win over the Vikings. They recorded six sacks and six takeaways in those games and the defensive effort on Monday bought their offense time to get going after a poor start to the game.

Linebacker Greg Rousseau had a sack in each win to get to eight for the season and he said the performances show a unit that is discovering its identity.

"Last week wasn't a fluke," Rousseau said, via Lance Lysowski of the Buffalo News. "It's what we are. It's what we can do. We just have to keep going."

The counter to Rousseau or anyone else feeling bullish about the Bills defense is that Joe Fagnano was at quarterback for most of the Ravens game and that Carson Wentz was running the Vikings offense. The Bills can't control such things, of course, but they do make it harder to feel like the results were all about tweaks that had improved the defense.

General Manager Brandon Beane has a chance to bolster the group before Tuesday afternoon's deadline and games against the Jets and Dolphins offer chances to keep building confidence over the next two weeks. Those things could help because the real tests of the Bills defense won't come for some time.

#2947. Brent crude falls below $90 for first time since August on Iran war de-escalation hopes

International oil benchmark Brent Crude fell below $90 a barrel for the first time since August on Tuesday as comments from U.S. President Donald Trump fueled hopes for an end to Washington's nearly nine-month conflict with Iran.

Brent, the price gauge for around 80% of global crude, was 2.65% lower at $90.14 at 5:33 a.m. ET after contracts with January expiry dipped below $90 earlier in the morning.

U.S. WTI Crude was down 2.4% at $84.78 a barrel.

Trump said on Monday that the war with Iran could end "fairly soon" and that Tehran was "talking very politely" with Washington.

"We're seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it's going to be ending fairly soon," he said at the White House following a meeting with Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani. "Iran militarily is effectively over," Trump told reporters.

Trump also said in a Truth Social post that Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait would "prefer the status quo," namely maintaining a naval blockade against Iran and preventing the country from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials.

Crude oil prices have been highly volatile this year, proving sensitive to any perceived shift in direction in the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran.

Brent Crude started the year around $60 a barrel before soaring as high as $130 a barrel as military strikes escalated in March and April. Prices retreated in June and July before climbing back to those levels as the conflict increasingly appeared entrenched.

Crude oil flows through the key Strait of Hormuz waterway have largely recovered. But consumers have suffered from resulting volatility in energy markets, as wider global conflicts — including Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and the Russia-Ukraine war — exacerbate a shortage of refining capacity, sending prices of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel soaring.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance have both acknowledged that public disapproval of the Iran war and high energy prices played a role in the Republicans' punishing result in the U.S. midterms last week.

While officials on both sides have continued to trade hostile words, particularly as they debate control of the Strait of Hormuz, the U.S. had largely held back on military strikes since September, with Trump saying in early October they would not resume until after the midterms.

The U.S. carried out what Trump called "minor strikes" on Iran after reports that two missiles struck Qeshm Island, located near the Strait of Hormuz off the country's southern coast.

Analysts were divided on how the U.S. administration would approach the Iran conflict after the Democrats' resounding midterm victories, with some viewing escalation as a strong possibility despite the initial market reaction suggesting hopes of a deal.

"The market has continued to unwind some of the geopolitical risk premium built into prices in recent weeks as expectations grow that the conflict between the US and Iran could move towards de-escalation," ING strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson said in a note Tuesday.

"Signs that regional oil flows are recovering have added to the downward pressure... Reports that Iran may be softening its position on control of the Strait of Hormuz have also reduced concerns over a prolonged disruption to one of the world's most important oil transit routes."

"For now, the return of more Gulf barrels and the prospect of easing tensions are taking some of the geopolitical premium out of crude. However, with regional negotiations still uncertain and infrastructure risks persisting, we expect oil prices to remain sensitive to developments in the Middle East."

Fereidun Fesharaki, chairman of energy consultancy FGE, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Tuesday that, despite market moves, he still did not see any prospects of a peace deal between the U.S. and Iran.

"The difference between the two sides is so wide, it cannot be bridged. Most importantly, the U.S. wants all the nuclear material, enriched material, to be transferred out of Iran, and there is no way that the Iranian regime would agree to this, and there is no way the Iranian regime would agree to let the Strait of Hormuz be open for a free flow of oil the way it was before the war," Fesharaki said.

"So, with these two in between, I just can't see a deal being made.

"Trump has to decide. Either he says, 'I declare victory and walk away,' or he goes to war. If he goes to war, he's got only a window of two weeks from today for himself and for [Israeli Prime Minister] Netanyahu, or there will be no war at all on a long-term basis," Fesharaki added.

Netanyahu's political party failed to win a majority in Israel's election last month, with rival Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of the Israel Defense Forces, officially tasked with forming a government on Sunday.

— CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this story.

#2945. Bears working out Jeffery Simmons' former Titans teammate

The Chicago Bears are once again looking to make moves at defensive tackle. According to ESPN's Adam Schefter, the Bears are hosting free agent Jordan Elliott for a workout on Tuesday.

It's the first time Elliott is meeting with a team since he was released by the Tennessee Titans last month after he went to his car to retrieve a gun after an argument with Titans offensive tackle JC Latham. Defensive lineman John Franklin-Meyers helped deescalate the situation, but it was a move that cost Elliott his job in Tennessee.

Titans head coach Robert Saleh said Elliott is a good person who had "a terrible lapse in judgment." He hoped Elliott would get another opportunity in the NFL, and we'll see fit hat comes in Chicago.

Perhaps a big part of the Bears exploring the possibility of bringing Elliott onboard after that incident is due to his former Titans teammate Jeffery Simmons, who Chicago recently acquired in a trade for a pair of first-round picks.

Elliott is a former third-round pick by the Cleveland Browns, who's also spent time with the San Francisco 49ers and most recently Titans. He's started 65 games and totaled 159 tackles, 11 tackles for loss, five sacks, 14 QB hits and five pass breakups.

This potential move is likely due to the loss of rotational piece Kentavius Street, who suffered a season-ending knee injury in a Week 8 win over the Seattle Seahawks. Elliott would provide solid depth along the defensive line and serve as a reunion with Simmons.

#2944. TSMC's October sales jump as global chip boom rolls on

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. on Tuesday reported October revenue of 586.89 billion New Taiwan dollars ($17.88 billion), up 59.7% from a year earlier and up 14.7% from the previous month.

The world's largest contract chipmaker benefited from strong demand for advanced semiconductors, as major technology companies continue to invest heavily in artificial intelligence.

Last month, TSMC reported a record third-quarter net profit of NT$763.1 billion, beating estimates while revenue came at NT$1.49 trillion.

The chipmaker expects capital expenditure from 2026 to 2028 to be significantly higher than in the previous three years as it continues to invest to support customer demand. Its third-quarter operating margin reached 58.7%, exceeding the upper end of its guidance range of 58%.

TSMC shares closed 2.24% higher on Tuesday, amid broader market volatility in Taiwan. The island's financial regulator last week announced tighter short-selling restrictions that took effect Monday, cutting the daily limit on intraday short-selling orders from 30% to 3%.

Separately, Taiwan's exports surged 58.9% in October from a year earlier to $96.76 billion, according to government data released Monday. Strong demand for advanced chips helped drive a 61.4% increase in electronic components exports, local media reported, citing the finance ministry.

#2942. Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.

The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.

Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.

In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.

For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.

John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.

"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.

Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.

Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.

Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.

Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

#2941. Trump sees opening for Ukraine peace deal, but key questions remain ahead of Abu Dhabi talks

President Donald Trump said there was increasing willingness from both Russia and Ukraine to end the war, as representatives from Kyiv and Moscow headed to Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for the first peace talks since February.

Speaking to reporters at the White House on Monday, Trump said both sides were battle-weary, more than four and a half years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

"We're also seeing a very strong inclination to end Russia and Ukraine [war]," Trump said ahead of the U.S.-brokered negotiations, adding that, "We're involved in that because I want to see people stop getting killed again."

His comments followed a U.S. official’s assessment that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing some flexibility over a possible exchange of territory, according to Reuters.

A senior Ukrainian official, however, rejected suggestions that Kyiv was considering territorial concessions, telling Reuters that any discussion of territory would have to take place between national leaders and be accompanied by appropriate security guarantees.

Russia has publicly maintained its demand that Ukraine surrender the entire eastern Donbas region, including territory Moscow has not captured.

William Courtney, former U.S. ambassador to Kazakhstan and Georgia and adjunct senior fellow at RAND, told CNBC's Dan Murphy on Tuesday that there are "no signs thus far" that the Kremlin is showing any willingness to negotiate seriously towards a ceasefire milestone, which he considers a logical "first step."

He noted that Ukraine's proposal for a ceasefire along the current battle line would accept Russia's de facto control of occupied territory without formally recognizing it, calling it a concession by Kyiv, and said it was puzzling that Trump stopped backing the proposal after Putin objected at their Alaska meeting last year.

Courtney also pointed to Russia's continued missile and drone attacks and efforts to destroy bridges over the Dnieper River, arguing that Moscow's aims toward Ukraine had not changed. He said serious talks would be unlikely without a shift in Russia's objectives or on the battlefield.

In his nightly address late Monday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged Washington to convince Russia to end the war and said recent Ukrainian battlefield gains and mounting Russian losses had improved Kyiv's bargaining power.

U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are set to lead Washington’s mediation efforts, while Russia has said Putin aide Vladimir ​Medinsky will serve ⁠as Moscow's chief negotiator ​at the Abu Dhabi talks, where postwar security guarantees for Ukraine are expected to feature prominently.

Courtney said such guarantees are issues for further into the future, after a ceasefire has already been agreed on. "It looks like because Russia has objected to a ceasefire proposal that Ukraine and the U.S. earlier last year made, that the Trump administration is no longer trying to achieve a ceasefire, even though that's logically the first step," he said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that discussions had advanced on a possible postwar security framework for Ukraine and Europe.

"Nothing's been finalized yet, and maybe some progress can be made in Abu Dhabi," Rubio said.

The renewed diplomacy comes amid continued fighting and mounting questions over the scale of Russia's wartime losses.

Belarusian Cyber Partisans, an opposition-linked hacker group, said its analysis of data it claims was obtained from Russia's state statistics agency identified 393,881 deaths linked to military operations or their consequences between 2022 and August 2026.

The group said its count was based on death records explicitly coded as resulting from hostilities or their consequences. It acknowledged that the figure could include civilians and deaths connected to other conflicts, while excluding personnel who are missing but have not been declared dead.

Rosstat has acknowledged that it was targeted in cyberattacks but denied that its databases were compromised, according to a Russian media outlet Kommersant. The hackers' claims and the underlying dataset have not been independently verified in full.

Separately, the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that 400,000 to 450,000 Russian military personnel were killed between February 2022 and June 2026.

At the upper end, that would be more than nine times the combined Soviet and Russian military fatalities in wars since World War II, according to the think tank.

The Moscow Times, citing a broader analysis of the leaked records, reported that roughly 450,000 war-related deaths would make the conflict Russia's fourth most common cause of death since 2022. The newspaper said it had cross-checked a sample of names, but could not verify the data set in its entirety.

#2939. Bengals Tuesday Trenches: Super in Spain, SNF and more

The Cincinnati Bengals won their fourth game in a row on Sunday morning in front of a national audience from Santiago Bernabéu Stadium in Madrid, Spain, by a score of 34-17.

Now, at 6-2 along with Pittsburgh, the Bengals are set to host the Steelers for what kind of feels like the AFC North title game even though we're only in Week 10.

The Bengals were almost perfect on offense. They scored on six of their eight drives (I'm not counting the last drive in which they could have scored but were able to kill the clock), and four of those scores were touchdowns. Joe Burrow completed 24/29 passes for 271 yards and three touchdowns — two to Tee Higgins and one deep bomb to Ja'Marr Chase to cap off their first drive of the game.

The defense had its moments, but the familiar struggles were there too. In the end, the Falcons' offense just couldn't hope to keep up, even though they seemed to hang around a little, especially early in the second half. Still, it never felt like the Bengals were potentially going to lose control of the game.

Here are some random thoughts on their three-score win before we get into the Steelers game:

Tee Higgins is a monster. He didn't have a ton of yards (32), but he caught two touchdown passes, and multiple passes—including one of those touchdowns—with guys draped all over him. Higgins looks like a man among boys when he catches the ball in traffic.

Ja'Marr Chase is a generational talent. His ability to turn into a running back as soon as his hands touch the ball is remarkable. He breaks tackles like a running back and has 220 yards after the catch so far in 2026. What I'd really like to see, though, is a yards-after-contact stat for him.

The offensive line held up beautifully against the Falcons, who came into Sunday morning's game with 18 sacks and weren't too far behind the Bengals. Burrow was sacked twice, but one of those sacks was much more of a coverage sack than anything to do with the line. If they can continue to protect Burrow like they did Sunday, the offense can break records.

The run game finally made an appearance on Sunday. To be clear, I think Burrow can beat about any defense with Chase, Higgins, and the other weapons he has, but it's hard to win in the playoffs if you can't run the ball. The Bengals were able to kill the clock with a solid running game in the fourth quarter. Chase Brown had multiple explosive runs, including one for 19 yards—a season-long for the Bengals' offense.

Dexter Lawrence. That's it. That's all I have to say.

Okay, a bit more: Lawrence didn't show up on the stat sheet much, but he lived in the backfield and forced Michael Penix into throwing early or on the run. He almost caused an intentional grounding penalty at one point. It's amazing how much one man can change the face of a defense.

The Bengals were unable to sack the quarterback on Sunday. This was their first game without a sack, and hopefully it's their last game. Cashius Howell is on IR, and the Bengals pretty much relied on Boye Mafe and Myles Murphy. Cedric Johnson only played 13 snaps, and Shemar Stewart played just 10. It would be nice to see a little more rotation to help keep the starters fresh.

Regardless of DJ Turner's PFF score, remember the receiver he's covering doesn't get targeted very often.

Money Mac strikes again—good from 57 and 43 yards, and that 43-yard kick in the fourth quarter put any hope of a comeback out of reach for the Falcons.

Speaking of the Falcons, we can credit the Bengals for breaking Atlanta—The Falcons traded Jessie Bates Monday morning.

I honestly don't think it's an exaggeration to say that Sunday night's game against the Steelers at Paycor Stadium is one of the biggest games to be played there in the last several seasons. The Steelers are also 6-2, and with the injuries in Baltimore and the Browns doing Browns things, it's not crazy to think the winner of this game likely wins the division.

The Bengals are not the same team they were that lost to the Steelers in Week 3. The offense is awake and clicking. The defense has its moments, but could use some help. Tuesday (today) is the last day they can make an addition via trade, as the deadline is at 4 PM Eastern. I highly doubt the Bengals make a move, but I also highly doubt they'd trade a first-round pick for Lawrence. Can they pull off another trade just five months after the Lawrence trade?

If there was a time to do it, it's now. The Bengals are in prime position to make a run, and they obviously need a little help, especially on defense, to get things right. They could use depth at cornerback as well as linebacker. They could probably get by without any additions on offense, but adding Jonathan Taylor sure would be cool.

The Bengals are favored by 3.5 points, which is a half point over home-field advantage, and a win would put them at 7-2 with a firm grasp on the division, and a handful of winnable games before they host the Chiefs in a little over a month.

This is where we hoped the Bengals would be at this point in the season.

#2938. Former Royals catcher and manager Bob Boone dies at age 78

Bob Boone, a four-time All-Star catcher who spent two seasons as a player with the Kansas City Royals before managing the club for parts of three seasons, has died at the age of 78, according to a social media post from his family. The son of All-Star infielder Ray Boone, and the father of All-Star infielders Bret and Aaron Boone, the Boones were the first family to have three generations of MLB players.

Bob Boone was one of the most accomplished defensive catchers of his generation, winning seven Gold Glove Awards over a 19-year playing career. He was originally drafted by the Philadelphia Phillies after a standout career at Stanford. He he finished third in Rookie of the Year voting and was a three-time All-Star with the Phillies. He faced the Royals in the 1980 World Series as a catcher for the Phillies, hitting .412 (7-for-17) in the series for his only championship.

He moved onto the Angels in 1982, helping them win the division in their first year, earning MVP votes, and winning a Gold Glove. He was an All-Star the next year, and over seven years in Anaheim, he set the club record for most games behind the plate.

He left Anaheim and signed with the Royals in 1989 at the age of 41. He appeared in 131 games and hit .274/.351/.323, winning his seventh Gold Glove and finishing with 2.4 rWAR. After 40 games in 1990, he retired.

After the 1994 season was cancelled during the work stoppage, the Royals hired Bob Boone as manager to replace Hal McRae and usher in a new youth movement. Despite trading away stars like David Cone and Brian McRae, the Royals were in the hunt for the new "Wild Card" spot for most of the season, until a poor September caused them to fall under .500 at 70-74.

Boone was a very cerebral manager, but would frequently clash with the media. He was criticized for constantly changing the lineup, and for employing "Boonieball," as then-Kansas City Star columnist Jeffrey Flanagan would call his style of play. Boone finished just 75-86 in 1996, and was fired at the 1997 All-Star break after a 36-46 start, replaced by Tony Muser.

Boone would later manage the Cincinnati Reds from 2001-2003, although he never managed them to a winning season. He joined the Washington Nationals front office in 2005 and served the team until he retired in 2021.

#2937. Victor Wembanyama nearly had a historic 40-point triple-double in just 25 minutes of blowout win over Suns

The Phoenix Suns had absolutely no answer for Victor Wembanyama on Monday night.

And he wasn't even on the court for that long.

Wembanyama finished just shy of a triple-double while leading the San Antonio Spurs to a blowout 122-96 win over the Suns at the Mortgage Matchup Center. But instead of a traditional points-rebounds-assists triple-double, Wembanyama finished just one block short of that mark.

He put up 40 points in the win, and had 11 rebounds and 9 blocks to go with 3 assists in just his 25 minutes on the floor. It would have been the third time in his career that he's logged a triple-double with blocks, following an outing in the Western Conference semifinals last season where he had a NBA playoffs-record 12 blocks against the Minnesota Timberwolves. Wembanyama also pulled off the same feat in 2024, and is the youngest player in league history to do so.

Wembanyama is now just the second player in league history to ever record multiple games with at least 40 points, 10 rebounds and 8 blocks in a single season, joining Wilt Chamberlain. Wembanyama had a similar stat line in a win over the Mavericks earlier this month where he finished with 52 points, 24 rebounds and 8 blocks, which he did in 34 minutes.

According to The Athletic's Jared Weiss, there are only nine other players in NBA history to ever have at least 40 points, 10 rebounds and 8 blocks in a single game. The fewest minutes anyone else has ever needed to hit that mark was 38. Chamberlain is the only other player to do so with less than 20 field-goal attempts.

Since 1980-81, only one player — Sleepy Floyd on Feb. 26, 1991 — scored 40 points in fewer than Wembanyama's 25 minutes, 21 seconds.

Wembanyama was incredibly efficient throughout the night. He missed just four of the 19 shots he took, and had 22 of his 40 points in the first half. That gave San Antonio a 15-point lead at the break.

In the third, Wembanyama grabbed his seventh block and just shrugged his shoulders at Ryan Dunn as the ball went flying out of bounds. He then followed it up with a wild finger roll in which he took off from just inside the arc moments later.

The Spurs didn't need to keep Wembanyama in the game much longer after that. They pulled him early in the final period as they cruised to the 26-point win without any issue.

Before he left for good, it even looked like he was just toying with the Suns. They simply couldn't stop him.

Devin Booker led the Suns with 32 points while shooting 10-of-17 from the field. Khaman Maluach added 11 points off the bench, though they were the only two Suns players to hit double figures. The Suns have now lost five of their last seven games, and sit at 3-6 on the season.

Dylan Harper had 17 points to go with Wembanyama's 40-point outing. De'Aaron Fox finished with 15 points and nine rebounds, too. The Spurs now sit at 9-2 after Monday's win, which marked their ninth straight after dropping back-to-back games to open the season.

Wembanyama is only 11 games into his fourth season in the league, and it's still early November. But he is already making a big statement in the MVP race as the Spurs get the jump in the Western Conference. If Wembanyama keeps this up, they are going to be a very, very hard team to beat in a few months.

#2936. Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.

Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.

Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.

Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.

Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.

Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."
