#2935. Jim Cramer says Anthropic's IPO could make or break the AI trade. Here's why

Anthropic's upcoming initial public offering could be a crucial test of investor confidence in the artificial intelligence trade, CNBC's Jim Cramer said on Monday.

"Without it, I don't see how the AI-related stocks can make a real recovery," the "Mad Money" host said, exactly two weeks after the Claude developer filed its S-1 IPO paperwork. Despite the recent sell-off in AI stocks, Anthropic is reportedly moving ahead with its IPO plans. The company is expected to meet with major investors this week and is targeting a trading debut as early as Thursday or Friday of next week, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. "I don't think it's hyperbolic to say that this could be one of the most consequential IPOs in history."

Cramer explained that the billions of dollars being spent on AI chips and data centers ultimately depend on a handful of AI developers, including Anthropic, generating enough revenue to justify those investments.

"Anthropic is important because it is one of just a few companies at the end of the food chain for all of the AI data center investments that we've seen, so it is one of the few companies that, ultimately, needs to make money from all of this investment spending," Cramer said. "If it can't do that, or if it cannot convince enough investors that it will do so, then it's tough to justify all of the AI investments that are being made today."

Cramer pointed to SpaceX as an example of how interconnected the AI trade has become. Much of the Elon Musk rocket and AI company's recent revenue growth has come from renting computing capacity to customers, including Alphabet's Google and Anthropic. Google pays roughly $900 million a month for that capacity, while Anthropic's commitment has grown from an initial $1.25 billion monthly to more than $3 billion, according to its IPO prospectus.

Those contracts allow for SpaceX's massive purchases of Nvidia chips. "But if an Anthropic deal fails?" Cramer said. "Then Anthropic wouldn't have the cash to fulfill its contracts, and you'd have to take down estimates for both SpaceX and Nvidia, along with a whole host of other compute providers to Anthropic, and their suppliers." Not to mention, Alphabet, Amazon, and Nvidia have all invested in Anthropic, making their earnings sensitive to changes in the AI developer's valuation.

The wrinkle here is that investor appetite for an Anthropic IPO appears to be weakening. Anthropic's potential valuation has reportedly fallen from as much as $2 trillion earlier this fall to as low as $1 trillion following last week's technology sell-off on concerns that the Democratic wave in the midterm election will mean slower new data center construction.

On Friday, during the CNBC Investing Club's Annual Meeting, Cramer also stressed the importance of the Anthropic offering to the AI trade and to Club portfolio names Alphabet, Amazon and Nvidia.

#2932. Game Recap: Victor Wembanyama scores 40 as Spurs defeat Suns 122-96

What flavor do you like your popcorn? Are you a traditional butter person? Or do you look forward to the holidays, when the Chicago mix makes its annual appearance, and you're treated to that glorious combination of cheddar and caramel popcorn? Because on Monday night against the San Antonio Spurs, you might as well have grabbed a bag of your favorite popcorn, settled into your favorite chair, and enjoyed the show that is Victor Wembanyama.

Coming off an electrifying 52-point performance last week that included 24 rebounds and eight blocks, Wembanyama followed it up with another spectacular showing, this time at the expense of the Phoenix Suns, as San Antonio cruised to a 122-96 victory.

Wemby was the story. Plain and simple. He finished the evening with 40 points on an absurd 15-of-19 shooting, adding 11 rebounds and eight blocks. And here's the part that makes those numbers even more ridiculous: He accomplished all of that damage in a mere 25 minutes of action. You know how we like to track Khaman Maluach's restocks per 36 minutes around here? That wonderful combination of rebounds, steals, and blocks that helps quantify a big man's impact? Well, Wembanyama posted 27 restocks per 36 minutes in this one.

Devin Booker certainly did his part to keep the Suns afloat, scoring 32 points on 10-of-17 shooting from the field. He also added four assists, a steal, and a block while committing zero turnovers. Unfortunately, no other Phoenix starter scored more than seven points to help him out.

Against a team like the Spurs, you need to be able to shoot the three ball efficiently to have a chance at competing, and the Suns simply couldn't do that. They ended 9-of-26 from deep, good for 34.6%. They only turned the ball over 7 times. But they were blocked 10 times.

San Antonio has now won nine consecutive games and sits at 9-2 on the season, while the Phoenix Suns have fallen to 3-6.

The whistle was blown pretty liberally to start the game, as Victor Wembanyama drew three shooting fouls within the first five minutes. San Antonio's early game plan was clearly to attack the basket, knowing the Suns lacked a significant shot-blocking presence on the interior. Meanwhile, Devin Booker once again catalyzed Phoenix's offense, scoring the team's first nine points.

Booker's presence was certainly felt throughout the first quarter, and his impact was evident on both ends of the floor. His best sequence began with a defensive breakup of an alley-oop attempt to Stephon Castle. He then went down to the other end and knocked down a three-pointer over Victor Wembanyama.

Devin Booker finished the first quarter shooting 5-of-8 from the field and 2-of-3 from beyond the arc, scoring 15 of the Suns' 25 points. But the Spurs capitalized on all three of Phoenix's turnovers, converting them into seven points while outrebounding the Suns 14-9. San Antonio took a 31-25 lead into the second quarter.

The momentum carried over as the Spurs extended their run to 12-0 across the two quarters, pushing Phoenix's deficit to 11 points. With Devin Booker taking a breather, the Suns opened the second quarter shooting 1-of-6 from the field and 0-of-4 from beyond the arc through the first 2:37. Meanwhile, the Spurs were a perfect 4-of-4 from the field, including 1-of-1 from deep, and suddenly Phoenix found itself trailing by 14 points.

The Suns were -12 in the non-Booker minutes in the second. From 1:23 in the first to 7:59 in the second, the Spurs put together a 21-2 run.

With 5:19 remaining in the second quarter, the Suns found themselves trailing by 20 points.

Then, with 1:54 left in the first half, Keldon Johnson delivered an unnatural kick on a layup attempt that caught Devin Booker square in the junk, the same type of play that got Dillon Brooks ejected last week. Yet the officials opted not to even review it. Funny how that works, isn't it?

Over the final eight minutes of the half, Phoenix was +3 with Booker on the floor, but the Suns were ultimately outscored 30-21 in the second quarter. Booker finished the half with 23 points.

Meanwhile, Victor Wembanyama had 22 points on 7-of-8 shooting from the field and 7-of-8 from the free-throw line. He also added six rebounds, three assists, and five blocks, leading the Spurs in all of those statistical categories. At halftime, San Antonio led Phoenix 61-46.

The Phoenix Suns opened the second half with a much-needed infusion of energy, finding opportunities to attack in transition and briefly put pressure on the San Antonio Spurs. After an opening three-pointer from Julian Champagnie, Phoenix responded with an 8-0 run to cut the deficit to 10 points. But getting that close seemed to flip a switch for Victor Wembanyama, as San Antonio answered with a 10-4 run of its own to regain control. Before long, the Suns found themselves staring at another 20-point deficit.

Phoenix had another frustrating offensive quarter and again failed to reach 25 points. The Suns collectively shot 8-of-26 from the field and 3-of-9 from beyond the arc, struggling to generate any consistent offensive rhythm. Devin Booker led the way with nine points, while Dillon Brooks contributed five. The rest of the roster? A miserable 3-of-14 from the field.

Meanwhile, San Antonio continued to demonstrate why it's one of the most dangerous teams in the Western Conference. Dylan Harper erupted for 14 points in the third quarter, adding three rebounds and an assist, while Wembanyama contributed 10 points, four rebounds, and a block. Every time Phoenix appeared ready to make things interesting, the Spurs had an answer, methodically dismantling whatever momentum the Suns managed to generate.

By the end of the third quarter, Phoenix trailed 93-68, facing a 25-point deficit and another uphill battle that was becoming increasingly difficult to overcome.

The fourth quarter? Well, the Suns essentially waved the white flag with eight minutes remaining, pulling their starters and allowing Jamaree Bouyea and Rasheer Fleming to see the floor. Cam Spencer, Koa Peat, and Duop Reath followed shortly thereafter, as Phoenix found itself trailing by 30 points and the outcome was all but decided.

There were at least a few entertaining moments from the young guys. Peat, the Suns' rookie, wasted little time making an impression, executing a smooth spin move before finishing off the glass. On the very next possession, he connected with Jamaree Bouyea for an alley-oop, providing a brief spark of energy as Phoenix trimmed the deficit to 26 points.

At that stage, moral victories were about the only thing left to celebrate. Suns lose, 122-96.

The Suns are right back at it tomorrow night as they host the Clippers. We shall see you then.

#2930. Senate advances Trump-backed bipartisan bill to speed critical infrastructure projects

The Senate on Monday advanced a bipartisan bill that aims to significantly speed up the approval process for critical U.S. infrastructure projects.

The vote, 73-25, allows the Senate to begin debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act bill as it heads toward final passage

The bill, which would reform the permitting process for projects, has emerged as a key priority of Congress' lame duck session. President Donald Trump, who often opposes bipartisan legislation, has endorsed the package.

The legislation would amend laws like the National Environmental Policy Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act to speed up the review process that hinders the buildout of resources like electricity generation, while also overhauling the process for greenlighting transmission lines.

The bill would also force artificial intelligence companies and data center developers to pay their own way for power and grid enhancements.

Republicans have long argued that environmental laws are too restrictive and hinder the U.S. from building big things like power plants and mines. Democrats, meanwhile, want to speed up the buildout of clean energy projects like solar and wind to lower carbon emissions

Lawmakers have circled a deal to streamline the nation's complex web of permitting laws for years, but most prior efforts have sputtered. This year, negotiators believe they will catch lightning in a bottle and make BAAJA law before this Congress ends in January.

The lawmakers are touting further tailwinds after last week's elections, where Democrats wiped out Republicans and seized majorities in both chambers of Congress

"Just one week ago Americans sent a clear message: They want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable. That's precisely what this permitting reform bill will do," said Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the top Democrat and likely incoming Chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, during a Monday morning press conference.

The bill would still require approval by the House of Representatives if it is able to pass the Senate this week. Trump's endorsement of the effort is likely to help the bill get a vote in the House if it clears the Senate.

#2929. As AI becomes more fractured, one name stands out: AMD

As Anthropic rushes to takes its shares public, the AI trade is showing cracks, and they are not confined to fringe players.

We recently wrote about CoreWeave, which fell 15.5% on Oct. 14 as yields on its 2032 notes touched 15%, and its default-swap spreads nearly doubled in October. IREN is down more than 20% this year. Last Thursday, the contagion reached chipmakers, which makes sense since much of CRWV and IREN's spending is going there. AMD dropped 8.1% as Meta's financing plans and a supply warning from Lam Research exacerbated data-center fears about the pace of AI spending.

Because when you screen for factors that demonstrably generate outperformance over time, the list narrows quickly. My screen: price above the 200-day moving average; revenue growing at least as fast as the S&P 500 (5%+ per annum); EPS growing at least as fast (7%+); rating upgrades; a PEG below 3; and ROE and ROIC of at least 12%. Of the names reporting in the next two weeks, AMD is effectively the only one that makes the list. Yes, you can (and arguably should, as our staples article described) position your portfolio with slightly less tech exposure than the broad indices provide, but we can't ignore the market's biggest and most transformative sector entirely.

Especially because the growth in this case doesn't just meet my criteria; it blows past them. Consensus for Q3 calls for EPS of $1.94 on revenue of $13.06 billion, versus $1.20 and $9.25 billion a year ago. That's YoY growth of nearly 62% and 41%, respectively. The recent drawdown came from a sector selloff, not anything AMD reported, but it shows that if some names in the space get hit, even the larger players are likely to feel it. On Oct. 6, Lisa Su said AMD would substantially increase supply in 2027 because AI orders keep outrunning capacity.

So how do you balance factors we know work for a fast-growing company against a backdrop of cracks in the AI trade? Options.

Owning the stock outright means absorbing a roughly 9% to 11% implied earnings-related move (day of). Earnings are about a week out, and over the past four quarters the smallest move over a similar window was more than 9%, and the largest move, after the company reported its Q1 26 results, was 38%! Of course, that kind of volatility means options aren't cheap, and that rich premium is also a reason not to simply buy calls.

A call spread risk reversal does both jobs: it reduces risk if the cracks widen, and the short options offset the elevated volatility we would otherwise pay for. The bottom chart shows that, by sacrificing about $1,700 of upside for $5,000 in outperformance during a severe downside move, and given how jittery this trade has been lately, this is a way to stay in it with considerably less risk. $5,000 less, specifically. Of course, selling that out will tie up some cash, but less so than simply buying the stock. And selling both the out and the call reduces long call purchase by 66%

#2928. France blames Iran for supermarket refrigerator cyberattacks, weighs sanctions

France is "not ruling anything out" in its response to October's mass cyberattacks on supermarket refrigerators that the country has blamed on Iran, the country's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Tuesday.

The French government summoned Iran's ambassador Tuesday morning after Paris said Monday that the findings of an investigation laid the blame for the hacks on Shahid Kaveh, an affiliate of the cyber unit of the powerful Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Barrot told radio station Franceinfo that the French government could respond with bans on entering European territory and the freezing of assets of anyone held responsible, as it looks to deter any further malicious acts conducted against the region.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it categorically rejected the accusations made by France, labeling them "baseless and malicious."

"This latest round of allegations — a continuation of previous, repetitive claims — is clearly intended to divert public attention from France's own destructive policies toward Iran and the West Asia region. Such a move is highly irresponsible and contemptible; it is a transparent attempt to tarnish Iran's image and disrupt its relations with other nations," the MOF said in a statement, according to Google translation of the original Farsi.

Remote hacks on around 700 grocery stores over the night of Oct. 11 to Oct. 12 caused refrigerators and freezers to heat up by as much as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit).

The soaring temperatures spoiled food and sparked fires, generating tens of millions of dollars in damage. Major French retailers, including Intermarché, E. Leclerc, Carrefour, Monoprix and Coopérative U were targeted.

The Paris Prosecutor's Office is seeking international arrest warrants, Paris chief prosecutor Laure Beccuau said in a statement.

Investigators found use of Farsi and IP addresses pointing to devices in Iran, according to the statement, which added that the attacks were committed to serve a foreign power, in this case, Iran.

The hacks targeted refrigeration controllers supplied by Danfoss and Dixell, with attackers remotely taking control of the equipment through web interfaces and starting unlimited defrost cycles while disabling the safety alerts on sensors designed to activate when temperatures exceed a set threshold, it said.

The French government also said Monday that it would propose new European sanctions against any Iranian entities and individuals involved, and summon the Iranian Ambassador.

"France condemns in the strongest possible terms the unacceptable cyberattacks carried out on its territory by the Islamic Republic of Iran against its interests," France's Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

"This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory."

"This actor poses a persistent threat to our critical infrastructure. These destructive cyberattacks are unjustifiable, inexcusable, and violate international law," the ministry said.

CNBC has contacted the Iranian government for comment.

France attributes several previous cyberattacks on the country to Iran-based actors, including cyberattacks and "information manipulation campaigns" against the newspaper Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the Paris Olympics in 2024. Those led to sanctions in March 2026 against private Iranian company Emennet Pasargad.

More supermarket fridges elsewhere in Europe were targeted in November, with stores across Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Finland, Ireland and Sweden reporting losses.

French blood banks were also affected on Nov. 2 by cybersecurity attacks, the French Blood Establishment said.

Temperature and defrost thresholds at cold storage units used to store blood products and samples headed to healthcare settings and biobanks were "set to excessively high levels," the EFS said in a statement translated from French to English by CNBC.

European leaders and the public have meanwhile been rattled by a wave of hoax bomb threats that have caused dozens of passenger flights to perform emergency landings.

"It feels like this could be a pretty unsubtle message from hostile actors to European governments warning that..[they] have the capability to interfere with critical infrastructure and disrupt essential services whenever they choose," Simon Edwards, CEO of cybersecurity testing lab SE Labs, said in an emailed comment.

"Whether this is an attempt to intimidate governments or preparation for something bigger, it shows how vulnerable our infrastructure can be."

"The lack of basic cybersecurity hygiene is the key factor making these attacks possible, why were these fridges connected to the internet in the first place, and accessible without passwords?"

— CNBC's Emma Graham and Sawdah Bhaimiya contributed to this story.

#2927. Ripple strikes deal with Robinhood to expand its RLUSD digital dollar

Ripple has struck a deal with Robinhood to expand the reach of its digital dollar, RLUSD, strengthening trading and financing links between their institutional businesses and improving Robinhood's internal money management.

The partnership involves using RLUSD to settle institutional trades, automate Robinhood's treasury operations and expand access to digital asset trading and financing through Ripple Prime and Bitstamp, the global crypto exchange acquired by Robinhood last year.

It also helps meet Robinhood's ambition of becoming a global financial superapp, centralizing its customers' financial lives while expanding the underlying infrastructure that can serve both retail and institutional clients.

"Utility is what moves stablecoins forward. Working with Ripple, Bitstamp and Robinhood will have access to RLUSD for institutional settlement, Ripple Treasury for our operations and Ripple Prime for financing," Robinhood Crypto General Manager Johann Kerbrat said in a statement shared with CNBC. "That is what a connected, global financial system looks like."

Stablecoins have long been a workhorse of the crypto world, giving traders a way to move money among exchanges, buy and sell crypto assets, and park funds between trades without having to convert back into traditional currency. But as the crypto industry evolves beyond trading and markets move toward 24/7 liquidity, stablecoins are becoming essential financial infrastructure because of their ability to enable near-instant settlement and move dollar-denominated value at any time, regardless of traditional banking hours.

As firms look to do more with stablecoins beyond simply listing them on exchanges, stablecoin issuers are betting they'll favor a one-stop-shop approach that bundles the technology and services needed to move money, settle trades and manage cash.

"Stablecoins have evolved from a crypto trading tool into a critical piece of financial infrastructure," Ripple President Monica Long told CNBC. "The clearest evidence of this is where they're now being embedded — from corporate payments to capital markets. Our partnership with Robinhood reflects that evolution."

"This is about much more than trading," she added. "It's about fundamentally changing how money moves and is managed — giving institutions the ability to operate 24/7/365, unlocking liquidity and putting capital to work more efficiently."

Circle Internet Group, a Ripple competitor, is positioning itself for a similar future, where winning platforms, in addition to issuing stablecoins, also provide the infrastructure to put them to work. Earlier this year, for example, it launched the Circle Payments Network, connecting financial institutions and payment providers using its flagship USDC stablecoin and other digital assets for cross-border payments.

The network is Circle's answer to the 8-year-old Ripple Payments business, a service that helps businesses move money across borders, using any of several assets moving through that system, including USDC, Ripple-created XRP and, as of its debut in December 2024, RLUSD.

RLUSD's market cap has grown to more than $2.5 billion. Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC still dominate the total stablecoin market, which now exceeds $300 billion.

RLUSD will also be listed on Robinhood's trading platform, and is currently available to traders on Bitstamp as well as Robinhood Chain, the company's home-grown blockchain for tokenized stocks and other assets.

Robinhood, which reports third-quarter results for the three months ended in September after the market closes, rose about 2.5% in early trading Tuesday, snapping a three-day decline.

Correction: A previous headline misspelled RLUSD.

#2926. Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph won't make return in Germany

Kerby Joseph's season debut won't come on foreign soil.

Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said in his weekly radio interview on 97.1 The Ticket (WXYT-FM) that Joseph will not play in this weekend's game against the New England Patriots in Germany.

Joseph remains on the physically unable to perform list recovering from a cartilage condition in his knee that has kept him out of game action since last October. He returned to practice Oct. 28, and the Lions have until next week to activate him to the 53-man roster or keep him on PUP for the rest of the year.

Campbell has tempered expectations for Joseph's return, though both he and safeties coach Jim O'Neill said Joseph had a good week of practice last week.

The Lions traded for backup safety Andre Cisco on Monday, Nov. 9, adding him to a position group that includes starters Brian Branch and Chuck Clark, rookie backup Keith Abney and special teams player Christian Izien.

BIRKETT: 10 players Detroit Lions could target for upgrades

"It gives us flexibility," Campbell said of the Cisco trade. "That's what it does do is Cisco's obviously safety, he played nickel, he can play other things on third down in your dime package. So can Branch. We get Kerby back eventually here, Kerby gives you flexibility, you keep him where you need him or move him back and forth."

The Lions (6-2) play two games in five days once they return from Germany, against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Nov. 22 and the Chicago Bears on Thanksgiving. O'Neil said last week the team had not determined how to work Joseph back in the lineup once he is activated to the 53-man roster.

Campbell touched on a couple other topics in his weekly interview Tuesday.

Asked about Christian Mahogany's benching last week for violating team rules, Campbell indicated Mahogany has done that multiple times this year.

"That's why I have team rules, that's why we have team rules and we all got to abide by them, and if it's broken multiple times, then you do something about it," Campbell said. "We're on good standing and like I said, the ball's in his court. It'll be good."

Asked how Mahogany has responded since his benching, Campbell said, "Listen, we're good. We're all good. He'll be fine."

"Look, if you say you're going to do something, you better hold up to it or otherwise you're going to lose the respect of people around you," Campbell said. "Because if I'm sitting in that seat and I say one thing and then I don't do it, I'll immediately lose respect for that person. So we stick by what we say we're going to do here."

On Tuesday's NFL trade deadline, Campbell did not directly answer a question about whether the Lions are close to making any more deals, like they were two years ago when news of the Za'Darius Smith trade broke during Campbell's radio interview.

"No, we're not going to trade for Za'Darius, and as of right now there's nothing that I've heard in the last 10 minutes," Campbell said.

When asked a follow-up about whether the competitiveness of the NFC North makes it more likely the Lions will make a deal, Campbell said, "Oh yeah, we're going to get ready to go. We're going to have our best game plan in all three phases and we're going to be ready to get after New England's ass. I cannot wait."

The NFC North is the only division with all four teams above .500. The first-place Chicago Bears (7-2) added Pro Bowl defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons in a trade last month, the Minnesota Vikings (6-2) are believed to be in the market for quarterback help, and the Green Bay Packers (6-3) are expected to get top pass rusher Micah Parsons back from a torn ACL soon.

#2925. Trump says Iran war to end 'fairly soon,' plays down prospects of new strikes

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the war with Iran could end "fairly soon," adding that Tehran was "talking very politely" with Washington.

Trump told reporters in the White House Monday, after a meeting with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, that "We're seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it's going to be ending fairly soon."

"Iran militarily is effectively over," Trump said, citing the destruction of its navy and surging inflation that he said has hollowed out its economy.

Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait would "prefer the status quo" which involves maintaining the naval blockade against Iran and "Operation Iron Gate" — a task force announced on Saturday aimed at preventing Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials — Trump said in a Truth Social post.

He reiterated that Iran would not be allowed to have a nuclear weapon and kept the door open for potentially resuming strikes should circumstances change. "America is 'docked and loaded' and ready to go," he said, though caveating that new strikes were "quite unlikely."

The conflict, now in its ninth month, has driven a surge in fuel prices, hitting nearly every sector of the global economy.

The U.S. had reportedly planned for a potential increase in naval forces in the Middle East in the run-up to the midterm elections, with Trump hinting at escalating the conflict after the results.

The administration has since toned down the war rhetoric after bruising midterm election results that saw Republicans lose both chambers of Congress as voters expressed frustration with soaring living costs stemming from the war.

A diplomat briefed on the Qatar meeting told Axios that Trump told Al Thani that he wanted a deal and would give talks a chance, but could reverse course if Iran does not take the negotiations seriously.

Iran has put forward a two-day proposal to the U.S. via Qatari mediators, Reuters reported, citing a senior Iranian official, demanding lifting of the sanctions imposed on Tehran and a new shipping route in the Strait of Hormuz. Washington was reviewing the proposal, according to the report.

Iranian officials have disputed that talks with Washington were underway. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, reportedly said that Washington should stop "manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks."

Oil prices edged lower on Tuesday on the prospect of de-escalation, extending losses from the previous day. U.S. West Texas Intermediate dropped over 1% to $85.8 per barrel, after sliding more than 4% in the prior session. Brent futures dropped more than 1% to $91.56 a barrel, hovering near 10-week low levels.

#2924. San Antonio vs. Phoenix, Final Score: Spurs blot out the Suns, 122-96

In a tale of two (positive) San Antonio (9-2) halves, Victor Wembanyama put his dominant stamp on a 61-46 first half, and second-year guard Dylan Harper shined brightly in a 32-22 third period to inflate a 15-point halftime cushion to more than 30 in the 122-96 win. Instead of doing it over the second and third periods as it did in previous games, the Spurs put up 30+ point quarters through the first three quarters to build and hold its sizable advantage and moved to 3-0 on the road trip.

Wembanyama (40 points, 11 rebounds, and 8 blocks) asserted himself from the tip to put Phoenix back on their heels early on. Harper (17 points, 5 rebounds, and 4 assists) impressed with his smooth stroke and increasing confidence as San Antonio put the game out of reach in the third quarter. De'Aaron Fox (15 points, 9 rebounds, and 6 assists) did the bulk of his damage in the first half. Other double digit scorers included Julian Champagnie (11 points) and Harrison Barnes (11 points), and all Spurs that saw the court tonight again scored.

Devin Booker's otherworldly mid-range shooting (32 points and 4 assists) prevented the Suns from being eclipsed fully in the first half. However, no other Suns joined him in double digits until Khaman Malauch (11 points) did well after the outcome was decided.

Perennial star Booker (nine) was the entirety of Phoenix's offense over the first 5+ minutes. Though they didn't shoot particularly well, the Spurs secured and maintained a slight lead by more conventional means as their outside shots were not finding their mark. Champagnie, in particular, had to find his seeing eye in the paint before knocking down a triple. A seven-point burst by Wembanyama enabled the Spurs to leave the quarter up six.

Wembanyama figured into nearly every part of an opening 10-2 run to start the second period. The lobbing problems – willingness and competency – that plagued prior Spurs squads seemed long gone as the superstar center put up a nearly perfect shooting line from the field (6-6) and line (5-6) only 15 game minutes in. After a couple of free throws, Booker (19 of 38) still had half of his team's output. San Antonio got its lead as high as 20, and more importantly – did not relinquish much of it – as it went to the break up 61-46.

Phoenix found more sure footing on offense to start he third, but the unfazed Spurs executed well in the halfcourt. Harper, in particular, showcased a pair of stepback jumpers, and topped those with a sublime floater on the left baseline to help extend the San Antonio lead to 19. After Harper's fourth and fifth buckets of the quarter, Jacob Tobey noted he "is just in his bag right now." His sixth basket evoked shakes of Michael Jordan's post game. Wemby's 16-foot finger roll capped a dominant third quarter clapback by San Antonio and they went to the fourth ahead by 25.

Fans of the three guard line-up will find a healthy amount of validation in Michael Pina's article today for The Ringer.

Carter Bryant entered action later in the first half and encouragingly willed home a transition three. His second three in the fourth quarter splashed home.

Collin Gillespie's Tough Sequence: In the opening minute of the fourth, Gillespie tried the Steve Nash move on Wembanyama and had his turnaround swatted away, and then his follow-up jumper was deflected, as well. To add insult to injury, the Suns guard was dunked on by Wembanyama at the other end.

Dylan Harper Sequence of the Game: The only thing that prevented him from doing more damage in a 14 point third quarter blitz was twisting his ankle on a Suns foot in transition. All of his field goals in the frame came from different spots on the court, which is very hard to do.

Keldon's Kitchen: That moustache has staying power.

Sequence of the Game #1: In what is a very viable after timeout play late in the first quarter, Fox slithered through the paint and delivered a feathery lob to Wembanyama. On the next possession, Keldon Johnson looked like he left a floater several feet short until Wembanyama took the errant orb and re-directed it through the rim. #greatpass

Sequence of the Game #2: Minutes into the second quarter, Wembanyama appeared to be fooled by a pocket pass from a Brooks pass to Igodaro – only to meet the Phoenix center at the rim to prevent a sure two points, and when Brooks tried to sneak a floater in after an offensive rebound, he, too, was turned away.

Sequence of the Game #3: It only took one possession in the second half for the Spurs to generate another highlight play – this time, Wembanyama found Fox at the dunker spot, and the guard whipped a behind the back pass to the left baseline to Champagnie for a corner three. It's worth watching possibly a dozen times.

Area 51 Sequence of the Game: Wembanyama and Castle orchestrated a beautiful two-man game late in the half that culminated in a Castle one-handed slamma jamma.

Tarris Reed, Jr. (lithe AND bruising big man) playing time: The big man (4 points, 1 rebound, 1 block, and 3 fouls) was an active presence in his eight minutes of playing time.

Fox and Harper scored San Antonio's first two buckets no more than three combined feet from the rim. Castle sand Champagnie put up goose-eggs over the first 5+ minutes, but Wembanyama, Fox, and Harper picked up the slack. Before the viewing audience could blink, Booker had put up 12 of the Suns' 14 points. An Igodaro baseline dunk provided some relief from the Booker scoring barrage. After successive bricks, Champagnie banked home a jumper in the paint to secure his first points. Tshe other Suns started contributing offensively and Khaman Malauch's surprising corner three tied the game. Wembanyama paired two lobs with an encouraging catch-and-shoot three to help San Antonio go up 31-25.

An opening 8-2 burst to start the second put San Antonio up a dozen. Wembanyama's fifth straight bucket – the prettiest to that point – was a baseline fade that Hakeem Olajuwon would have been proud of. After Johnson found Wembanyama for yet another lob, Sean Elliott exclaimed "What a change! Our guys have really figured out that lob!" Wembanyama then turned away Phoenix's lob attempt at the other end. Even after his first miss, Wembanyama snared the rebound and threw down a thunderous two-hand jam. Booker's next field goal caused Mitch Johnson to call a Pop-like timeout. Champagnie and Luke Kornet found each other on consecutive possessions to keep the lead near 20. Phoenix took advantage of the Spurs' hyper-aggressive perimeter defense to get cheap offense at the charity stripe. Booker took a shot to the nether regions on a Johnson bankshot that could be felt several states over. San Antonio ended its well-played half up 15.

A pair of triples from Champagnie and Fox prevented a tough third quarter start for San Antonio. Booker hit the 30 point mark 3 1/2 minutes in, and yet, the Spurs added to their lead. During one possession, Fox, Castle, and Harper occupied the left side (with Champagnie deep in the right corner), which allowed Wembanyama to go back door for a reverse lob from Harper. Johnson smartly fouled a runaway Igodaro and prevented a dunk while the Sun hit 1-of-2 from the line. Harper's flurry of baskets from different spots in and around the paint were what took away my breath this evening. San Antonio's run spanning the third and fourth quarters made it a no-doubt road win.

#2923. 6 potential Patriots targets ahead of the NFL trade deadline

The Nov. 10 4 p.m. ET NFL trade deadline is just hours away. Despite being just days removed from an ugly loss, the 5-4 New England Patriots still view themselves as contenders which could impact how they manage the roster.

"I want to see us do anything that we can with the roster that we have or potentially guys that aren't here, to continue to improve," head coach Mike Vrabel said Monday. "That's the focus here after nine weeks. We played some really good games, have been competitive, and then other days where it just wasn't good enough as a whole."

After trading a 2028 first-round pick this past offseason, the Patriots are not expected to make any significant investments. But the team does have additional Day 3 draft capital this year to add depth across the roster.

As for potential targets, here are six targets who could be on the radar.

The Patriots' run defense has trended in a positive direction in recent weeks, but adding Lopez could help the unit take another step forward. The 29-year-old has shown flashes of being a dominant run defender along the interior and would give New England another reliable option in the defensive line rotation. He is also under contract through the 2027 season for a reasonable salary.

Another option along the interior defensive line, Tomlinson has lost some of the pass-rushing juice he showed earlier in his career but remains a disruptive rotational piece. The 32-year-old is in the final year of his contract with the winless Chargers, with roughly $1.5 million remaining in cash owed to him. That makes him a potentially affordable option compared to Colts nose tackle Grover Stewart, who is owed approximately $6 million in cash. Tomlinson also spent the 2024 season with Mike Vrabel in Cleveland.

The Patriots have gotten strong overall production from Elijah Ponder, Dre'Mont Jones and Gabe Jacas along the edge. However, adding another pass rusher could help preserve that production down the stretch and bring some more juice to the unit as a whole. The former first-round pick, who has the size and athleticism New England has gravitated to on the edge, has served in a rotational role for the Cardinals this season and is in the final year of his contract, potentially making him an attainable deadline target.

The 2-7 Eagles continued to move pieces ahead of the trade deadline Monday, sending defensive tackle Jordan Davis to Jacksonville in exchange for a first- and second-round pick. Could former first-round pick Nolan Smith be next? Despite the Eagles' struggles, the 25-year-old has been productive, leading the team with 21 pressures this season while remaining a physical run defender. Philadelphia also exercised Smith's fifth-year option this past offseason, keeping him under contract through 2027 with under $14 million in cash owed his way. His age, production and contractual control could make him an appealing addition, although it may take a more significant investment than other names on this list.

New England's secondary was already without cornerback Charles Woods (hamstring) Sunday before fellow cornerback Carlton Davis (knee) left the game early. That left Christian Gonzalez and Marcus Jones with limited depth behind them, as rookies Karon Prunty and Channing Canada were the next options at cornerback. Former Patriot Jonathan Jones has settled into a rotational role with the Eagles, but still offers experience and man-coverage ability that could be valuable for a New England secondary dealing with injuries.

As noted above, the Patriots are without their 2028 first-round pick after sending it to Philadelphia in the offseason trade for A.J. Brown. While New England is focused on competing this season, there is still a bigger-picture argument for adding draft capital and getting younger across the roster. That probably is more of an offseason focus, but the team could explore the trade market to potentially move a veteran on the current roster if the right offer comes along.

#2922. AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.

Fears over artificial intelligence debt have eased after a bout of volatility. But more tests for AI debt are coming.

Oracle holds its Investor Day on Wednesday. And hyperscalers Alphabet and Amazon.com are scheduled to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.

Credit markets are on edge over a flood of AI debt, though fears have eased up a little lately. Meta Platforms' plans for a $95 billion stock offering, announced on Monday, helped bring down its credit-default swap spreads. Those spreads had risen last week when the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter. Other CDS spreads had moved higher too, though they have since backed off.

Investors had expected Meta to bring a large bond deal to market shortly after its earnings announcement, said Richard Cheng, head of Nuveen's investment-grade corporate sector team. The fact that it wasn't announced came as a relief.

"Just the absence of the bond deal itself is a direct catalyst for AI-related spread tightening," he said.

A credit spread is the difference in the yield between the corporate bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. When spreads tighten, it means investors are becoming more confident about the bond issuer.

The market action over the last few days shows that investors are recognizing that "credit fears may have been overblown," said CNBC contributor Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.

"I expect that these better feelings, maybe not good but better, may continue as companies announce their quarters over the next few weeks."

Still, spreads on CDS remain wider over the past year due to a surge of debt issuance and free cash flows turning negative across the AI space. Meta's CDS spread, for instance, is still up 177% year to date, while Amazon's spread has gained 129%.

"It's not necessarily fundamentals," said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin. "It's more, I'd say, 80% driven by technicals and sentiment."

Alphabet and Amazon pose the next big hurdle for tech bonds as they update their capex plans and free cash flow forecasts. Microsoft's earnings are also due Wednesday, but the company has yet to issue any bonds to pay for its AI spending.

Both Amazon and Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in the second quarter and analysts expect that trend to continue.

Analysts expect Alphabet to report free cash flow of -$2.3 billion while spending $55.2 billion on capital expenditures in the third quarter, according to FactSet consensus estimates. Amazon is expected to report -$9.9 billion in free cash flow against capex of $58.7 billion.

S&P Global Ratings estimated in an August report that the hyperscalers will have negative free operating cash flow in 2026 and 2027.

More critical will be their outlooks, Cheng says. "The singular focus on the investors' minds is really what the capex guidance trajectory looks like across the hyperscaler space."

Meeks believes elevated capex is a sign of strong AI demand. The hyperscalers have "decided that with all the evidence they have — and they have more than you and me — that this is worthwhile spending, and not just worthwhile; it's required," he said.

CreditSights' Chalfin doesn't expect the hyperscalers to announce major new bond issuance around their earnings reports. Oracle's updates may be more critical for credit markets. The company has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and is clinging to an investment-grade credit rating of BBB-, the lowest level of investment grade above junk, according to S&P.

"It's the most important IG tech credit, just given how it's a bit more stressed relative to the A-rated names," he said. "It's trading more like a high-yield credit, even though it's IG, and so there's just a lot of investor concern on that one."

One wrinkle to the AI debt story: balance sheets don't reveal the whole picture. The companies are using complicated off-balance sheet arrangements for data centers and chip financing, and they aren't fully transparent, S&P Global said in a September report.

"There are commitments they are entering into, for example, into data center leases or purchase commitments on chips that aren't necessarily treated as debt," Mark Habib, digital infrastructure sector lead at S&P Global Ratings, said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Monday.

S&P is trying to provide the market with more visibility on those commitments "to give a fuller picture of what kinds of obligations they're actually entering into," he added.

Oracle aside, hyperscaler credit ratings are all comfortably above A levels — reflecting the fact that they have broadly diversified revenue streams, ample coverage for interest payments, and capacity to add leverage if they choose.

Nuveen's Cheng isn't concerned, pointing out that while there has been some credit repricing, there is no credit crisis.

"They continue to have exceptional credit profiles, strong cash generation liquidity," he said of the largest hyperscalers.

"The market is really not concerned about credit quality at this point," Cheng added. "It's really just the trajectory of the capex needs and the supply of debt to fund that. Both of those are pointing in one direction — and that's up."

Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that Oracle's investment-grade credit rating is BBB-, according to S&P. A previous version mischaracterized the company's credit rating.

#2921. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#2920. Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph won't make return in Germany

Kerby Joseph's season debut won't come on foreign soil.

Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said in his weekly radio interview on 97.1 The Ticket (WXYT-FM) that Joseph will not play in this weekend's game against the New England Patriots in Germany.

Joseph remains on the physically unable to perform list recovering from a cartilage condition in his knee that has kept him out of game action since last October. He returned to practice Oct. 28, and the Lions have until next week to activate him to the 53-man roster or keep him on PUP for the rest of the year.

Campbell has tempered expectations for Joseph's return, though both he and safeties coach Jim O'Neill said Joseph had a good week of practice last week.

The Lions traded for backup safety Andre Cisco on Monday, Nov. 9, adding him to a position group that includes starters Brian Branch and Chuck Clark, rookie backup Keith Abney and special teams player Christian Izien.

BIRKETT: 10 players Detroit Lions could target for upgrades

"It gives us flexibility," Campbell said of the Cisco trade. "That's what it does do is Cisco's obviously safety, he played nickel, he can play other things on third down in your dime package. So can Branch. We get Kerby back eventually here, Kerby gives you flexibility, you keep him where you need him or move him back and forth."

The Lions (6-2) play two games in five days once they return from Germany, against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Nov. 22 and the Chicago Bears on Thanksgiving. O'Neil said last week the team had not determined how to work Joseph back in the lineup once he is activated to the 53-man roster.

Campbell touched on a couple other topics in his weekly interview Tuesday.

Asked about Christian Mahogany's benching last week for violating team rules, Campbell indicated Mahogany has done that multiple times this year.

"That's why I have team rules, that's why we have team rules and we all got to abide by them, and if it's broken multiple times, then you do something about it," Campbell said. "We're on good standing and like I said, the ball's in his court. It'll be good."

Asked how Mahogany has responded since his benching, Campbell said, "Listen, we're good. We're all good. He'll be fine."

"Look, if you say you're going to do something, you better hold up to it or otherwise you're going to lose the respect of people around you," Campbell said. "Because if I'm sitting in that seat and I say one thing and then I don't do it, I'll immediately lose respect for that person. So we stick by what we say we're going to do here."

On Tuesday's NFL trade deadline, Campbell did not directly answer a question about whether the Lions are close to making any more deals, like they were two years ago when news of the Za'Darius Smith trade broke during Campbell's radio interview.

"No, we're not going to trade for Za'Darius, and as of right now there's nothing that I've heard in the last 10 minutes," Campbell said.

When asked a follow-up about whether the competitiveness of the NFC North makes it more likely the Lions will make a deal, Campbell said, "Oh yeah, we're going to get ready to go. We're going to have our best game plan in all three phases and we're going to be ready to get after New England's ass. I cannot wait."

The NFC North is the only division with all four teams above .500. The first-place Chicago Bears (7-2) added Pro Bowl defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons in a trade last month, the Minnesota Vikings (6-2) are believed to be in the market for quarterback help, and the Green Bay Packers (6-3) are expected to get top pass rusher Micah Parsons back from a torn ACL soon.

#2919. Trump’s C-SPAN call marks latest surprise post-midterm appearance

President Donald Trump made an unexpected call into C-SPAN's evening broadcast Monday, extending a series of surprise appearances after Republicans' midterm election defeat.

"It looks like we've got a call from the White House," host Mimi Geerges told viewers as Trump joined the debut of "Washington Journal Primetime."

Trump congratulated Geerges on the launch before taking questions on immigration, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Iran war.

Asked what he watches on C-SPAN, Trump said he follows viewer call-ins to gauge public sentiment.

"I like to watch the call-ins because it gives me a little of an indication of where we are," he said.

The unannounced, eight-minute call followed another unexpected appearance earlier Monday, when Trump entered the White House briefing room alongside UFC CEO Dana White. Reporters were summoned so quickly that aides did not have time to attach the presidential seal to the podium, according to Reuters.

It was Trump's first briefing room appearance in 198 days, according to a White House pool report. With the press secretary post vacant, Trump joked about offering White the job, to which the UFC chief declined.

Trump said he had been having "a very bad press day," as he floated White as his next press secretary.

Last Wednesday, a day after Republicans suffered substantial midterm losses, Trump also abruptly invited reporters to the construction site of his White House ballroom for his first public event since the election.

Trump spent more than 20 minutes discussing White House construction and renovation projects, including the ballroom's Corinthian columns, marble flooring and the helipad, before turning to the election results during questions from reporters.

When asked whether he regretted how his campaign had ended, Trump distanced himself from the Republican losses.

"If I were on the ballot, we would have won," he said.

Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the Nov. 3 elections, dealing Trump a major political setback and setting up a divided government when the new Congress takes office in January.

Trump has long favored direct telephone contact with the media, including live calls to Fox News programs such as "Fox & Friends" during his first term.

CBS News previously reported that Trump personally arranged one such television appearance, while The Associated Press has documented his habit of contacting journalists directly by cellphone to pitch stories and react to live coverage.

— CNBC's Daniel Mangan contributed to this story.

#2917. Discussion: What is your dream trade deadline move for the Detroit Lions?

Welcome to NFL trade deadline day. After 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, no more trades can be executed until the start of the league year in 2027.

For the Detroit Lions, that likely means this is their last opportunity to make a roster upgrade for the 2026 season. And while the Lions don't have any massively pressing needs, they are in a bit of an arms race in the NFC. The Chicago Bears added DT Jeffery Simmons a couple of weeks ago. The Seattle Seahawks added guard Quenton Nelson. The 49ers brought back DeForest Buckner.

Detroit is in a good spot in the NFC—currently holding onto the fifth seed in the NFL playoff standings—but just about everyone in contention for a postseason spot is playing decent football right now.

The Lions have already made one minor move before the deadline, trading for reserve safety Andre Cisco. But I'm guessing most Lions fans want more. So today's Question of the Day is:

My answer: Trading for Eagles linebacker Zack Baun.

Philadelphia has already shown a willingness to trade amid their 2-7 start to the season. On Monday, they sent defensive tackle Jordan Davis to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a first-round pick and a future second-round pick. That's a pretty penny to pay, and it may be indicative that Baun will be costly if the Eagles are going to let him go.

But in Baun, the Lions would be getting a dynamic playmaker. Baun does everything in that Eagles defense. He's above average in coverage—grading 71.4 or better in each of the last three seasons, per PFF. He's a pass-rushing threat, with nine sacks since 2024. And he's an absolute force in the run game, as well.

He'd also come with an insanely team-friendly contract, seeing as most of his money is currently tied up in signing and option bonuses that stay with the Eagles upon a trade. Detroit would only be due a prorated version of his $1.215 million salary this year, then they would have an option for 2027 to pay Baun a $14.4 million option bonus to keep him around in 2027.

Now, that low salary would likely mean shelling out significant draft capital to lure him away from Philly. We're likely talking about a second-round pick, minimum. But if that's the price, I'd pull the trigger.

The Lions don't just have questions at linebacker this year—with Jack Campbell's future in football unknown, Jimmy Rolder on season-ending IR, and Devin White also on IR. But Detroit also has questions beyond this year. Only Campbell, Derrick Barnes, and Rolder are signed for 2027, and there's an out in Barnes' contract if Detroit wishes to move on. Baun would give the Lions a head start on fortifying their linebacker room for the future.

#2914. 5 Offseason Question for Pirates at GM Meetings

The 2026 MLB GM meetings are underway in Las Vegas. Typically, these meetings spark offseason buzz and rumors but don't produce much action. Instead, the groundwork for future deals is typically laid this week.

But this year is different. Teams and players are up against a ticking clock as a lockout is expected to take place once the collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1. The uncertainty surrounding this offseason could spark more aggressiveness and earlier action.

The Pirates have quite a few items on their checklist. Ben Cherington said at the end of the regular season that he will be ready to strike if something comes to fruition before the lockout.

Here are five offseason questions for Cherington and the Pirates.

The $60 million question? The $80 million question? Whatever the dollar amount is, it's by far the biggest question for the Pirates this winter.

It's been over a decade since Pittsburgh had a player of Lowe's caliber reach free agency. Lowe was sensational on both sides of the ball in his first year with the Pirates. He sparked a drastic offensive turnaround by leading the team in home runs and RBI and could win his first Silver Slugger next week. He also turned himself into a strong defensive second baseman.

The Pirates will face stiff competition to try and retain the 32-year-old. Lowe is one of the top free agents available this year and there are a lot of teams in the league have a need at second base. There has been a wide range of contract predictions for what it might take to sign Lowe. But if the Pirates want him back, they'll have to shatter their franchise free agent contract record (three years, $39 million).

The logical option would be to slide Nick Gonzales back to second base if Lowe signs elsewhere. Gonzales was one of seven MLB players this season to bat .300 but struggled defensively in his first season at third base.

But the free agent third base market is not particularly strong. Japanese star Teruaki Sato tops the list, followed by options such as Alec Bohm and J.P Crawford. The Pirates went to the trade market to land Lowe last offseason and it might make more sense to go that route again should Lowe depart. Top trade options include the Astros' Isaac Paredes and the Athletics' Zack Gelof.

If the Pirates did explore a second baseman, there are some solid options available in free agency. Jazz Chisholm Jr., Luis Arraez and Gleyber Torres are among the fallback options.

While most of the attention will be on Lowe and second/third base, the Pirates do have several other needs on their roster.

Topping the list is a left-handed relief pitcher. Mason Montgomery, Evan Sisk, Brandon Eisert and Hunter Barco are the only left-handers on the 40-man. Montgomery, who is the team's closer, is the only option that can be fully trusted. Gregory Soto is a free agent. Maybe the Pirates will think about re-signing him. If not, there are plenty of other options available.

After that, the Pirates should be looking for a right-handed bat to help solve some of their problems against left-handed pitching. A leverage reliever and starting pitching depth are among their other needs.

With talks of a potential salary cap and floor in the next CBA, the Pirates have been a hot topic this offseason. Owner Bob Nutting has developed a reputation as an owner who doesn't spend, and it's impossible to disagree with anyone who has that opinion of him.

The Pirates were more aggressive spending money last offseason than they usually are. They signed their first multi-year free agent (Ryan O'Hearn, two years, $29 million) in almost a decade. They added Lowe's salary via trade and signed Soto and Marcell Ozuna (whoops).

But the Pirates enter this offseason with a payroll that's already projected to be $100 million. That's not far off from their Opening Day payroll this year, which was a franchise record. Pittsburgh is closer to the playoffs than they have been any year in the last decade. Will Nutting open up his wallet to make a legit push?

One way the Pirates can create financial flexibility is by trading Mitch Keller. The veteran right-hander is owed $18.4 million next year and $20.4 million in 2027.

The Pirates flirted with trading him last offseason. In retrospect, they probably should have. Keller not only had his worst season since in five years but ended the year on the IL with a right arm teres major muscle injury. Teams will understandably be reluctant to take on Keller and his contract given what happened this season.

If the Pirates did want to trade Keller, they shouldn't expect much in return other than salary relief. Some other options for facilitating a deal include adding a prospect or other assets or eating some of the money owed to him.

#2913. $6.3 billion Binance hack is largest crypto theft on record

Binance said Friday that a security incident impacted about $6.3 billion in client assets, with around $3 billion frozen on-chain, marking the largest crypto hack on record.

The company later added it began recovering assets impacted by the breach after pledging to cover losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users, which the company created in 2018 as a protection for clients in the event of a hack.

It wasn't clear how the attack took place. The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions.

The FBI said Friday it was aware of the incident and was in touch with "relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate ​potential impacts, ​and ⁠coordinate appropriate investigative steps."

It wasn't clear either who was responsible for the breach. But TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, pointed to North Korean hackers as the potential culprits. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said in a post.

Blockchain data platform Chainalysis also said this appears "be the work of North Korean cybercrime group TraderTraitor. This group has repeatedly targeted the cryptocurrency industry, exchanges, DeFi protocols, and investors, to raise funds for the regime. We base our intelligence assessment on on-chain activity observed in the hours following the hack."

Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals while it overhauls its withdrawal security systems and has revoked the affected address authorizations, Teng said. The exchange is also working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the stolen funds, while deposits remain unaffected.

Binance co-founder Yi He said deposits remained unaffected and continued to operate normally, while the exchange was working on enhancements to its withdrawal service and related address controls. It expects to begin resuming withdrawal services within the next 48 hours.

"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak. We will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the facts are fully verified," Binance said.

The announcement followed moves by several crypto firms, including Circle Internet Group, Tether and Ripple, to freeze funds tied to the hack.

Exploits are not uncommon in the crypto space. In 2025, Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to a hack. More recently, Bitget lost more than $350 million worth of digital assets in a cyber theft incident. Over the past several years, bad actors have also drained billions of dollars in crypto from decentralized exchanges.

This week's breach "proves our exact point in proposing regulations for crypto markets earlier this month," Michael Selig, chairman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, said Friday in a CNBC "Squawk on the Street" interview. The U.S. derivatives regulator on Oct. 5 proposed a framework that would effectively put crypto exchanges under federal government oversight — after Congress failed to approve legislation to regulate the asset.

"The real issue here is that these are unregulated offshore exchanges, and they don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets here in the United States. We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cyber security safeguards that we have in our markets today," he said.

Bitcoin fell more than 4% to $77,187.60 on Friday as the hack weighed on crypto markets.

Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said Thursday evening in a social media post that the company had frozen more than 800 million in USD Coin associated with the incident. USDT stablecoin issuer Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino also said in on X that his firm had frozen more than 1.5 billion of its stablecoin that may have been related to a potential breach.

Jack McDonald, Ripple's senior vice president of stablecoins, said it was actively freezing affected funds held in RLUSD, its U.S. dollar-backed stablecoin.

#2911. 3 unexpected reasons the October jobs report was so strong

A little-noticed category in Friday's blockbuster jobs report is challenging the consensus view about job losses caused by artificial intelligence.

At least for now, the data suggests the U.S. is gaining jobs as a result of the AI boom, not losing them.

And another category suggests the strong jobs numbers could have some staying power.

Nonfarm payrolls grew by 165,000 jobs in October, according to the Friday report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It was a surprising surge in hiring that blew way past Wall Street's expectations. Economists polled by Dow Jones had forecast growth of just 59,000 for the month.

Here are three surprising things you might have missed from the report.

Hiring for consultants surged in the month, sending the profession's total head count to a fresh record.

The labor force for management, scientific and technical consultants expanded by 17,300 jobs between September and October, the largest month-over-month increase in nearly two years. This category is a subset of the professional and business services sector tracked by BLS and accounted for 25% of the entire sector's gains for the month.

What's more, this workforce has grown by more than 45,000 jobs over the past year. That gain pushed the total employee base for these types of workers past 1.9 million for the first time on record, according to BLS data.

Hiring in the industry had largely stalled since 2023 following years of rapid expansion during the pandemic. Wall Street has questioned if the rise of artificial intelligence will curb demand for these services.

Those fears have led shares of consulting firm Gartner to lose more than half of their value over the past three years. Accenture and FTI Consulting have dropped about 18% and 9% over that period, even as the S&P 500 has climbed roughly 74%.

Now, some economists are speculating that the recent jump could be driven by businesses hiring consultants to help them adopt AI. Gartner forecast in September that worldwide AI spending would total $2.7 trillion in 2026, a nearly 50% increase year over year.

"The AI buildout and corporate interests to increase utilization will keep the technical consultants employed," said Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial.

Roach called the consulting sector a bright spot in October that is "worth watching." He noted that these jobs also saw double-digit growth in the late 1990s, as firms raced to implement new internet technology into their businesses.

So far, data suggests that AI may be adding more jobs to the labor market than it is taking away through automation. An assessment by Moody's Analytics found that AI has created a net 786,000 jobs since ChatGPT launched in November 2022, driven in part by data center construction.

"Wasn't AI supposed to destroy jobs? The most dystopian scenarios even called for mass unemployment," Mark Zandi, Moody's chief economist, wrote in a social media post on Monday. "That risk hasn't gone away, and AI-driven productivity gains could still shift into a higher gear. But for now, AI is adding to job growth, not subtracting from it."

Hiring of temporary workers also drove growth, which could signal that the labor market is heating up.

The subsector's payrolls grew by 18,600 in October, one of its largest month-over-month increases since 2022. This category is another part of the professional and business services sector and accounted for 27% of the sector's gains for the month.

The total size of this workforce is still well below record highs set in 2022. But headcount has grown roughly 3% since December and now sits at levels last seen in April 2025, the month that President Donald Trump's rollout of his plan for steep tariffs put corporate America on alert.

Economists see temporary hiring as a leading indicator in the labor market. Conventional wisdom suggests that companies that hire new workers on a short-term basis often transition them to full-time roles later.

That could be what's happening here, but the fact that the end of the year is approaching makes it harder to tell. The boost could be a result of hiring as the holiday shopping season approaches — and if employers are staffing up for the holidays, they are less likely to retain those workers when January rolls around. Such hiring hasn't typically happened this early, but the season creeps earlier each year. The BLS adjusts its numbers to account for seasonal trends, but won't immediately make an adjustment if the trend is changing.

One hint that holiday hiring may be shifting comes in a separate category of workers: couriers and messengers. This is another area that acts as a barometer for holiday labor demand, and just over one out of every 10 new jobs in the month was in this category.

That category "bears watching for reversal in the months ahead," said Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy and research at Glenmede, a wealth manager.

Hiring related to political campaigns in the final weeks of an expensive election cycle could have also boosted payrolls.

Employment in political organizations has historically spiked heading into midterm or presidential elections, according to a BLS analysis. Staffing levels tend to peak in October of those years, the data shows. Nonfarm payrolls expanded in the months before the 2018 and 2022 midterm elections.

But the vast size of campaign coffers this cycle may have translated into more jobs than before.

The 2026 congressional election is slated to go down in history as the most expensive midterm on record, according to an analysis from OpenSecrets, a money-in-politics watchdog group. Billions of dollars spent on campaigns may have translated into paid gigs that involve door knocking, phone banking or other election-related work.
