#2909. The midterm election could reshape the muni bond market. Here’s what investors need to know

The outcome of Tuesday's election is expected to have broad implications across the market, including municipal bonds.

The spotlight has been on the battle for congressional control and whether Democrats will wrest the House of Representatives, the Senate or both from Republicans. But for the muni market, what happens at the state level could have bigger repercussions — at least in the near term.

There is an array of initiatives on ballots around the nation that could change tax laws and add to bond supply. Taxes matter to muni investors since the income received is free of federal tax, as well as state tax if the holder lives in the state where the bond is issued.

Depending on the location, ballot measures are up for approval that would either provide tax breaks, or raise taxes on the wealthy.

"It's a complete bifurcation between red and blue states," said Dan Close, head of municipals at Nuveen. "Blue states are trying to put in place graduated income tax structures, trying to capture more revenue from high-income earners. Red states are promoting affordability by trying to cut property taxes."

Red states are those that predominantly vote Republican, while blue states swing toward Democrats.

For instance, California has a proposition known as the "billionaire tax," which would impose a one-time levy equal to 5% of the wealth of certain taxpayers with at least $1 billion in assets. The state also has a measure on the ballot that would make a temporary tax hike permanent on individuals earning over $371,000, adjusted annually for inflation. The tax is currently set to expire in 2031.

"The impact to the muni bond market will be to make the exemption more valuable," Close said of the possible passage of tax increases. Investors will likely seek shelter in the muni market, which would send bond prices higher, he noted.

It is a different story in Florida, where voters are set to decide whether to increase the Sunshine State's homestead exemption for non-school district property taxes. Qualified homeowners currently have a $25,000 property tax exemption, as well as another for $25,000 that doesn't apply to school property taxes. The new proposal raises the latter exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 by 2028. New residents have a five-year waiting period before receiving the benefit.

If passed, some local governments will have to find other revenue sources or increase the overall tax rate to replace what they've lost, said Tom Kozlik, head of public policy and municipal strategy at HilltopSecurities.

"It's not necessarily going to result in downgrades for sure, but there would have to be some balancing with regard to overall revenues," he said.

Not all municipalities will be hurt equally, which means credit research is important, said Close.

"Like everything in municipal finance, it is really on a case-by-case basis that you could have some credit deterioration from [a] rollback of property taxes," he said.

Other voters on Tuesday will be asked to approve more state or local government debt. That could weigh on a market that has already seen heightened supply.

Some $473.8 billion has already been issued year to date, through September, according to the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association. That's a 7.8% increase over the same period a year ago. In 2025, total muni issuance reached $587.3 billion, 14.3% higher than 2024, Sifma said.

Cooper Howard, director of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research, believes supply is the biggest issue coming out of the election.

"That amount of issuance has been one of the reasons why you have to see that strong amount of demand continue to keep pace with it for total returns to keep up," Howard said.

Fortunately, new supply doesn't necessarily come quickly into the market. "There's a window over a couple years that they can issue," he noted.

The ultimate makeup of the next Congress could also have consequences for muni investors as lawmakers sort out their priorities. Most notable is what lawmakers will do to tackle the country's affordability problem, Kozlik at Hilltop said.

"There could be some tax policy initiatives and even affordability-related initiatives that manifest themselves in the first quarter of next year," he said. "That could impact housing. It could impact higher education. It could impact public power financing."

Investors considering moves before the election may want to look at those states with tax increases on the ballot, said Close at Nuveen.

For instance, Nuveen recently began offering a separately managed account dedicated to Washington after getting an enormous number of inquiries from financial advisors. The state recently enacted a 9.9% tax on individuals with taxable annual income above $1 million, set to go into effect in 2028. But the issue is now being put to voters, who can decide whether to repeal the new law.

"At the margin, if you do think that some of these measures are going to pass, knowing that bonds usually move up with an increase in taxes, there might be some opportunities to buy ahead of the election for blue states," Close said.

Howard believes munis are attractive right now, particularly for those who are in a tax bracket of 24% or above. Fundamentals are good and the bonds largely have good credit quality, he said. "About 70% of the broad muni index is either triple-A or double-A rated."

Kozlik is also bullish, calling yields "really attractive." He suggests investors concentrate on AA-rated or higher bonds.

"The muni space is part of the portfolio that most investors want," he said. "It helps them sleep well at night."

#2908. Bilt bets on local businesses, hospitality and major sports franchises, expanding beyond residential rewards

A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

Bilt is taking its residential property technology out into the neighborhood, announcing the launch of two new platforms designed to help local businesses and event venues attract customers and build loyalty. It is essentially taking the operating system it built for apartment rents and mortgage payments and deploying it across local area businesses, including hospitality, restaurants and sports venues.

The first offering, Neighborhood OS, is an artificial intelligence-driven system that works with restaurants, retail, gyms and other local businesses to attract customers, offer rewards and encourage repeat business. It does this by connecting the business's existing systems, like reservations and payments.

"We're helping local businesses tap into more commerce by being able to reach new customers and accept those rewards as currency to spend," said Ankur Jain, founder and CEO of Bilt. "This is giving every one of those merchants their own Shopify-like platform for real businesses, so now they can run their own marketing campaigns. They can run their own loyalty campaigns."

One example of this might be that a restaurant near a customer's home would offer a perk, then if the customer takes it, the system would recognize that and track that customer to manage future interactions, like more rewards, reservations or guest services. The AI helps the businesses measure which perks worked and which didn't.

Bilt lists initial partners that include Altamarea Group, AM Parking, Lowe's, and Thumbtack. Bilt says it partners with 50,000 merchants so residents can use Bilt rewards at their stores. Businesses that already have rewards systems don't need to replace them. This gives small and midsized retailers an AI platform to use on their own.

They can run marketing offers on their own to drive demand from buildings on the Bilt platform. Examples might be offering a customer a free round of drinks on their 10th visit or pulling in local sports fans by running a watch party on game day. They could push that out through the platform. So merchants now have the same tools that Bilt had to offer its own rewards.

"Offline commerce is six times larger in spend, and it's run by mom and pops, but they have to work across 10 different systems. Everything is done manually for marketing, and there's no way to track what's working," said Jain. "You democratize the ability for now mom and pop to sell against some of the biggest companies online, because they have all those tools."

The second offering is a membership platform for organizations that already have a customer base. That could be sports teams, property companies, hotels and financial institutions. The organization keeps its brand and customer relationship. Bilt layers in additional technology to connect that organization's program with its participating merchants, giving them access to more benefits they don't have through existing programs.

Bilt lists initial members including the Houston Rockets, Phoenix Suns, Sacramento Kings, Related Companies, Hyatt, Constellation Brands and Bozzuto, among others.

"We believe the neighborhood is one of the greatest amenities we can offer our residents," said Toby Bozzuto, president and CEO of Bozzuto. "Through our partnership with Bilt, we have an opportunity to make that amenity an even more meaningful part of their everyday lives."

For professional sports, the idea is to connect fans beyond the stadium. Teams will be able to introduce branded fan experiences that combine loyalty, fan passes, concierge services and neighborhood commerce. This would include rewards at local restaurants, retail businesses and branded events outside the stadium or arena.

Bilt launched in 2021 as a rewards program for rent and mortgage payments. Tenants could earn both loyalty rewards points as well as build credit history. It later expanded into credit cards. It reports 8.2 million members and powers one out of every four apartment buildings, according to the company.

#2906. Jazz Chisholm Jr. Faces Short Deal Path Like Bo Bichette

Jazz Chisholm Jr. is not going to get the same big money that Bo Bichette secured in free agency last year. Bichette left the Toronto Blue Jays for a three-year, $126 million pact with the New York Mets. The Bichette pact averages out to $42 million per year. The key to that massive contract was the opt-out clauses Bichette added after each season. He could have hit the open market this winter but chose to stay, and he holds that same power again next year. Chisholm now faces a similar path to get his value right, though the market looks much tougher for him.

USA Today's Bob Nightengale wrote a piece on Monday about ten free agents who will draw close attention soon. He looked specifically at Chisholm's situation and the idea of using an opt-out clause. Nightengale wrote that "He could be in for a rude awakening in the free agent market with executives openly wondering if anyone would give him more than a two-year contract." The Yankees did not make a qualifying offer to Chisholm, so he is now a free agent. This means teams can sign him without paying a draft pick to New York, but it also signals the team is ready to move on if the price is too high.

Despite the rough talk from front offices, Chisholm brings real skills to the table. He is a year removed from a 30/30 season where he hit 30 home runs and stole 30 bases. In 2026, he set a career high with 41 stolen bases in 50 attempts. That speed was a bright spot even if his overall hitting numbers were down. He has played second base since the trade from the Marlins and has graded out well there based on defensive metrics. He also has experience playing center field. His talent is undeniable, but teams worry about his consistency over a long term.

Nightengale noted that "No one can debate his talent. He may need an opt-out on any multi-year proposal so he can hit market again and re-establish himself." This strategy mirrors what Bichette did. If Chisholm signs for two years, he can prove he is healthy and hitting, then test the market again for a bigger deal. Various outlets have different guesses on what he might get. According to reports, Chisholm's potential deals are either 3 years/$110 million or 7 years/$185 million. Fangraphs, including Ben Clemens and the median crowdsource, has him at 4 years and $92 million. Kiley McDaniel sees a 2-year, $46 million deal with an opt-out, while MLB Trade Rumors has him at 2 years and $40 million with an opt-out.

The Philadelphia Phillies are one team that might make a move for him. Just Baseball's Ryan Finkelstein forecasts that Chisholm will agree to a two-year, $40 million deal with Philadelphia this offseason. For the 2027 season, Finkelstein stated Chisholm would earn $25 million, followed by a $15 million player option in 2028. Finkelstein wrote that "The best case for Jazz is likely a 1+1 deal where he can reset his market and have a pillow of a player option to fall back on." The Phillies have needed a boost for their offense, and adding Chisholm would give them more power in the middle of the lineup.

Rather than remaining in the American League, predictions suggest Chisholm will join one of this year's National League playoff teams.

#2905. Polymarket says annualized revenue has topped $1.8 billion

Prediction market platform Polymarket has surpassed $1.8 billion in annualized revenue, the company told CNBC on Tuesday.

That's up from June, when Polymarket disclosed that its annual revenue run rate was north of $1 billion, following the launch of its domestic exchange in May.

Polymarket's revenue is being fueled by growth in that U.S. exchange, which operates as a separate trading venue from its decentralized finance international platform. The domestic exchange saw more than $14.5 billion in notional volume in October, up from $4 billion in June, according to data analytics platform TickerTracker.

That increase has been driven by a series of highly traded events, including the FIFA World Cup over the summer and the start of the NFL season in September. Volume has been supported by the growing popularity of Combo event contracts, which work similarly to sportsbooks' multi-leg parlays, accounted for more than 70% of volume traded on the platform on Sunday.

The revenue growth since June also comes after the company began a fresh $1 billion funding round that values Polymarket at $21 billion.

Polymarket still faces near-term headwinds, though. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is conducting a broad investigation into the company, with questions surrounding advertising practices and whether the company in the past violated a settlement with the agency to bar U.S. residents from accessing its international exchange.

The company also may face increased scrutiny from a Democratic congress, partially due to the position of President Donald Trump's son — Donald Trump Jr. — as an advisor to the company.

But Polymarket previously told CNBC it would work with lawmakers as they begin to understand the growing prediction market industry. "We welcome scrutiny," a spokesperson said.

#2902. Bridgepoint sees opportunity in 're-rated' real estate

A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Alts newsletter, a guide to the fast-growing world of alternative investments, from private equity and private credit to hedge funds and venture capital. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

While higher interest rates are chasing many investors away from real estate, Bridgepoint Group sees growing opportunity in overlooked corners of the property market, according to company executives.

With $125 billion in assets, London-based Bridgepoint has expanded from core private equity and private credit into infrastructure, secondaries and real estate. This summer, it announced the acquisition of Kayne Anderson Real Estate, the real-estate investment firm with over $22 billion in assets.

In an interview with Inside Alts, Bridgepoint CEO Raoul Hughes said the acquisition gave the firm a "category-killing" real-estate offering as well as a bigger foothold in the U.S.

"All the products we have are the go-to products within their niche," Hughes said. "They're very entrepreneurial, very alpha-driven and we're all about real value-added investing. What we didn't have prior to coming together with Kayne Anderson was the real-estate piece."

Higher interest rates have created a new headwind for many real-estate funds. Funds that poured money into commercial and residential real estate in 2021, when interest rates were near zero, are now grappling with higher borrowing costs, compressed valuations, slower transaction volumes and more defaults.

Al Rabil, CEO and Co-Founder of Kayne Anderson Real Estate, said higher rates will lead to a shake-out in the industry. Disciplined investors with strong sector expertise will find new opportunities in the fallout, he said.

"People say 'oh interest rates up, real estate bad,'" Rabil said. "It's actually not quite that simple. Yes, interest rates are up, cap rates up, asset valuations down. But this is a longer duration investment business so it isn't day-to-day or quarter-to-quarter. When you get in an environment like the one we're in, it actually produces a very outsized investment opportunity because we're in very rarified air."

Rabil cited three real-estate sectors as being attractive for Bridgepoint and Kayne Anderson. Medical office space will continue to be an outperformer as the population ages. He said the asset class hasn't been below 90% occupancy in over 20 years, with demand far exceeding supply.

He said Kayne Anderson focuses specifically on the higher-margin sub-sectors of oncology, neurology, cardiology and diagnostics.

"People age 65 or over need seven times more doctor visits than those 45 and under," Rabil said. "So the population has a massive need for increased health care that has to be satisfied through medical office."

Another attractive sector is so-called "small-bay industrial," or commercial space used by small businesses and e-commerce retailers.

"Small businesses are 47% of GDP," Rabil said.

When it comes to residential, Rabil said higher interest rates could cause a reckoning. Investors poured billions into multi-family real estate in 2021 and 2022, with many of those loans financed with a 10-year Treasury at around 1%.

"Much of that debt is coming due today," he said. "There is a huge opportunity for very good assets that are structurally broken, in terms of the capital structure."

Hughes said that higher rates aren't likely to impact Bridgepoint's broader portfolio companies in private credit and private equity. He said the firm focuses on high-growth, high-margin businesses that are more resilient to interest rate swings.

"You'd rather rates were stabilizing where they are rather than going up," Hughes said. "And I think rates probably are stabilizing. But from an investing perspective, I don't think it materially damages our ability to drive returns from our equity portfolio."

#2901. Santoli: AI bull market almost surely needs tech stocks to recover to keep advancing

The road to bull-market glory does not run through Walmart and Berkshire Hathaway and Eli Lilly.

There's been a virtual buying panic in traditionally defensive, high-quality stocks over the past few weeks, a near-equal-and-opposite offset to the selling pressure in semiconductors and AI-build-out spenders. The three stocks above — the only members of the $1 trillion market-cap club not in Big Tech – have collectively added $550 billion in market value in the past month, almost making up for what Alphabet has lost.

The Nasdaq-100 and the S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV) are rushing toward one another in a satisfying picture of symmetry that nonetheless reflects an almost comical level of tactical rotation executed by an investment community accustomed to playing one factor against another.

While this to-and-fro has so far protected the S&P 500 as a whole from an appreciable setback for months, it has left it stymied around levels that date back to May — before we got two earnings-reporting seasons showing 30% annual profit growth.

A week ago here, I suggested the AI theme was nearing a make-or-break moment to stage a recovery or risk surrendering its leadership status and destabilizing the broader market. Thus far, this trade has failed to respond to moderate oversold conditions or a run of cosmetically strong hyperscaler quarterly results, further loosening its grip on the benefit of the doubt.

In stressed markets undergoing soul-searching about the long-term bullish thesis, prices often need to travel further to find buyers with conviction while the market action must disappoint dip-buyers to extinguish complacency. Hard to know if we're there, but presumably we're now closer.

The Nasdaq-100 closed Monday right at its 200-day moving average, off almost 11% from its record high. After an enervating failed Monday-morning bounce attempt, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index finished down another 3.8% and settled under the late-July low that was set as the Situational Awareness hedge fund was finished liquidating.

"Markets did not get the memo that bearish seasonal pressure typically subsides in mid-October and instead ended the month with some of the most acute selling pressure that has been realized during the late-summer/early-fall period," notes JPMorgan technical strategist Jason Hunter. He's advising clients to remain on the defensive "until we see clear evidence of a bottoming process on the charts or until there are clear signs of capitulation."

This is a time-tested playbook, though many a sharp market pullback has ended without what would qualify as unqualified capitulation.

The market action is winning some plaudits for the way non-tech stocks have held up better, many groups benefiting from the "quality" rotation while abandoned consumer cyclicals get a reprieve from easing oil prices and the slide in the 10-year Treasury yield back below 5%.

This gives active managers plenty to do in playing against a highly concentrated and tech-dependent S&P 500. But I'll continue to argue that the bull market built on the AI story will almost surely need the AI story to get back on track to keep advancing. A prolonged period when the equal-weight S&P 500 outperforms the market-cap-weighted version is otherwise known – usually – as a bear market.

The AI-related stocks' weighting in the S&P 500 is off the highs but remains near 45%, according to Morgan Stanley.

As the chart shows, AI has wobbled relative to the rest of the market during this uptrend before reasserting itself.  But there's a trickier element to the current gut check: In prior phases of the buildout, the key limiting bottleneck gave investors something to buy in order to exploit it.

The initial scarcity of GPUs meant to own Nvidia above all else from 2023 through 2024. When cloud capacity, power and cooling were found to be the crucial scarce resources, hyperscaler stocks worked and the AI-adjacent industrials were drastically revalued. Then memory emerged as the chokepoint and Micron and Sandisk went stratospheric.

Now, as Nvidia's Jensen Huang has said, capital is the constraint and that not only leaves no asset to buy, but it raises the cost of capital broadly as the mega-caps go free-cash-flow-negative.

Overlapping feedback loops and scrambled correlations across the markets and the real economy have further sapped investor conviction. Treasury yields no longer move with oil but largely with AI-capex sentiment, with both in retreat lately. AI-stock setbacks also mute inflation momentum and the equity wealth effect, meaning fewer Federal Reserve rate hikes are anticipated now versus a month ago.

This all probably sounds like an elaborate trap, and it has become one for the previously crowded trades. Could this reflect the end game for the AI-exuberance market chapter, which as I keep pointing out peaked around the SpaceX IPO in June? Impossible to say for sure, but if it were, I'm not sure things would look much different to this point.

But I don't want to dismiss the possibility that a lot of the known challenges are largely reflected in prices.

I argued in August that we should assume the valuation peak for this cycle was in. We've now retrenched to a forward P/E of 18.5 on the S&P 500 from 23 a year ago and the Nasdaq-100 at 20x is at the slimmest premium to the S&P 500 valuation in nine years. I'm on board with the idea that the market is telling us companies are now "over-earning," but if nothing else there is less valuation risk now than in recent months.

Sentiment toward AI stocks is in the dumps. Funds' positioning in tech has retreated below neutral. Important trading lows this year have happened near the turn of the month on March 30 and July 29, and the Nasdaq-100's relative-strength reading is exactly as oversold as it was at those turns.

So, stay alert for possible relief bounces that could evolve into something more consequential if indeed the midterm elections pass in a way that allows traders to unclench a bit into the year's home stretch.

John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "Similar to valuation, sentiment is not a timing tool, but it is getting harder and harder to find any bulls, as a near-perfect storm of tight financial conditions is being met with tech earnings that have gone from bad to worse in the blink of an eye."

-Another good big-picture conversation on the practical business and investment implications of the next phase of AI proliferation on Patrick O'Shaughnessy's Invest Like the Best podcast, this one with investor Cliff Sosin. His comparison of AI infrastructure economics to internet connectivity providers and his argument for how most of the productivity boost will go toward "consumer surplus" rather than corporate profits are particularly interesting.

-For my birthday Monday, my colleague and friend Sara Eisen wondered how I would write a birthday message to myself. I immediately regretted suggesting she ask ChatGPT, which generated this credible and somewhat embarrassing result:

"Another year older, though the longer-term trend remains constructive. Some modest deterioration in the underlying internals, perhaps, but nothing that suggests a decisive breakdown.

"The candles on the cake are approaching historically elevated levels, though valuation concerns have persisted for years without derailing the advance. At this stage, the key question isn't whether I've gotten older — that's largely priced in — but whether the wisdom gains can continue to offset the inevitable compression in energy multiples.

"For now, I'm maintaining a cautiously optimistic outlook, with upside optionality, downside support from family and friends, and no immediate need for Fed intervention. Happy birthday to me. The secular bull market remains intact."

The stampede into perceived defensive stocks has been a crucial driver of Apple shares' massive outperformance over the Nasdaq-100 since the AI-capex agita flared up months ago. Apple heading into Monday's earnings report had outperformed the Nasdaq-100 by nearly 20 percentage points over the prior six months.

Its singular refusal to join the aggressive spending binge to build AI capacity preserved its free cash flow and made it the perfect counterweight to the capex trade, while inflating Apple's valuation to a 15-year high.

But its advantage in free-cash-flow yield has now narrowed, thanks to its stock-price gains and the collapse of peer shares.

#2900. FIA boss looks to ‘end age limits’ for office holders – six months after ditching term limits

Mohammed Ben Sulayem is reportedly looking to end age limits for FIA office holders – just six months after the FIA president ditched term limits for those in leadership posts.

Emirati executive Ben Sulayem, 64, has been FIA president since December 2021 and was re-elected last year after other candidates were prevented from standing, due to quirks in the FIA statutes which meant the only prospective vice-president in one region was already aligned with Ben Sulayem.

Currently, FIA statutes rule out anyone over the age of 75 from standing for a presidential term. This rule was implemented in 2024 to "modernise the governance of the FIA and ensure that candidates for the presidency are more aligned with current leadership practices."

Yet just six months after Ben Sulayem ended term limits for those in leadership posts, the BBC reports that Ben Sulayem wants to discontinue the age-limit rule and put forward a proposal detailing as such to the FIA's General Assembly in Shanghai next month.

An FIA spokesperson told The Independent: "An age limit excludes candidates solely on the basis of their date of birth, regardless of their experience, expertise, or ability to contribute. Ultimately, the competent FIA bodies will retain full authority to elect the officeholders they deem appropriate."

"The proposal to remove age limits for FIA officeholders is one of the proposed amendments to the FIA Statutes to be put to the General Assembly in Shanghai in December. It was approved by the World Councils for submission in line with the process set out in the FIA Statutes, and will only take effect if the General Assembly votes in favour."

Ben Sulayem had originally introduced an upper age limit of 70 in 2023, in a move widely seen to prevent Motorsport UK boss David Richards from running.

Ben Sulayem, who is a regular in parc ferme and on the podium after F1 races, has overseen controversial moments in his near-five years in charge.

Ben Sulayem has clashed with Max Verstappen in the past (Getty)

His first term saw Ben Sulayem clash with Lewis Hamilton over the Brit's desire to wear jewellery in the cockpit, while he also angered drivers, including four-time world champion Max Verstappen, for issuing fines for swearing.

Last April, Robert Reid resigned as deputy president for sport, accusing the governing body of a "breakdown in governance standards." And presidential candidates such as Tim Mayer and Laura Villars were unhappy after they could not oppose him in last year's presidential elections.

FIA rules dictate a vice-president candidate must be nominated from each of its six global regions; Bernie Ecclestone's wife, Fabiana, the sole South American candidate, supported Ben Sulayem.

Meanwhile, Ben Sulayem has also voiced his support for end-of-season races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi to go ahead. A final call is expected on Tuesday.

The second-year star had 43 points in the Dallas Mavericks' 125-122 win against the Indiana Pacers on Monday, Nov. 9 at the American Airlines Center. He added 10 rebounds for a double-double and six assists with three steals for good measure.

According to the NBA, the 19-year-old joins Kevin Durant as the only other player in league history to have at least 40 points, 10 rebounds and five assists in a game as a teenager. ESPN adds that this is the 14th game in which Flagg has scored at least 30 points before turning 20 years old. Only LeBron James has more with 20 such games before he reached his 20th birthday.

Flagg had back-to-back dunks in the first quarter to cap an 11-0 run by the Mavericks. In one key play with less than 30 seconds left in the game, he dribbled against Andrew Nembhard, then drained a step-back jumper. The bucket extended Dallas' lead to four.

Kyrie Irving contributed 35 points for the Mavericks, while Pascal Siakam had 29 points, nine rebounds and eight assists for Indiana.

In April during his rookie season, the former Duke standout scored a career-high 51 points in a loss to the Orlando Magic. He won last season's Rookie of the Year award after averaging 21 points, 6.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists per game.

Flagg is averaging 24 points, 6.6 rebounds and 7.0 assists per outing this season.

He missed one game last month against the San Antonio Spurs due to a shoulder injury suffered in an earlier game against the Pacers.

#2897. Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses

Amazon's Ring is going deeper into surveillance with an indoor drone for home monitoring and an autonomous robot designed to patrol businesses.

The company on Tuesday unveiled the $250 Ring Drone Cam, a security camera that can fly from room to room, including upstairs, as well as capture footage during the day or at night. When an alarm or sensor on windows, doors and home security devices is triggered, the textbook-sized drone travels a pre-set path to investigate suspicious activity. Users can also deploy the drone at any time, the company said.

At a demo in New York on Monday, Ring CEO Jamie Siminoff said the drone could be used as a home monitoring tool and as a crime "deterrent" due to the device's built-in LED lights.

"If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window," Siminoff said. "You're probably not going to go into that house."

The drone, which can fly up to eight minutes at a time before autonomously returning to its charging dock, has two plastic-encased propellers that emit a loud buzz when it's airborne.

Ring devices have provided Amazon another avenue to grow its presence in the smart home beyond its Echo smart speakers and Eero routers, expanding in a market that Grand View Research estimates will top $200 billion in sales this year. It's equally fertile ground for Amazon rivals Apple and Google.

Ring first previewed its drone, then called the Always Home Cam, in 2020. Siminoff said he chose to hold off on releasing the device until Amazon could perfect the design, sensors and data processing.

The company on Tuesday also debuted the $1,000 Ring Rover Cam. The device repurposes Amazon's Astro home robot, which had a short life as a business device and has seen few upgrades since its 2021 debut, for companies to patrol offices, warehouses and other workspaces.

Ring said it "leveraged the best of Astro" to build the Ring Rover Cam, which it describes as a "purpose-built security robot."

Similar to the Astro, the device is a display mounted on a two-wheeled base with an extendable periscope camera. It also features a "built-in siren," two-way audio and a "light tower" that shines onto the ceiling to help users keep track of its whereabouts.

Siminoff said in an interview that the drone and the robot allow users to monitor multiple areas of their home or business with just one device.

"People like indoor cameras, but they don't necessarily want them everywhere around their home," Siminoff said.

Siminoff said the drone can't fly outside per Federal Aviation Administration regulations, which restrict operating drones unless they're within a line of sight of a pilot.

"We have told our customers not to do that because it's illegal," Siminoff said. "We've also put guardrails in there to make it so it doesn't fly outside."

The Ring Drone Cam ships in the U.S. on Jan. 27, pending approval from the Federal Communications Commission, while the Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping to users on Dec. 16, the company said.

#2896. How much you can make in 2027 and still pay 0% capital gains tax

The IRS has released the capital gains tax brackets for 2027, which include a six-figure earnings limit for the 0% rate for married couples.

If you're eager to sell profitable brokerage account investments, higher income thresholds for the 0% rate could help reduce your tax bill, experts say.

"The 0% capital gains bracket is easily one of the most overlooked strategies for tax-free income," said Stephen Maggard, a certified financial planner with Abacus Planning Group in Columbia, South Carolina.

But it's important to know how the tax brackets work and the possible trade-offs before selling investments.

Despite recent stock market volatility, many investors have portfolio gains after years of market growth. As of market close Nov. 9, the S&P 500 was up about 10% year-to-date. The index also returned more than 16% in 2025, and over 23% in 2024.

If you're planning to leverage the 0% capital gains bracket in 2027 to sell or rebalance brokerage account assets, here are some key things to know.

The capital gains brackets — with rates of 0%, 15% or 20% — apply to assets owned for more than one year, known as long-term capital gains. By contrast, investments held for one year or less are short-term gains, subject to regular income tax rates.

Your rate depends on taxable income, which you calculate by subtracting the greater of the standard or itemized deductions from your adjusted gross income, or AGI. Taxable income also includes any gains from investments that year.

The standard deduction will rise to $16,600 for single taxpayers and $33,200 for married couples in 2027.

For example, let's say a married couple's AGI is $130,000 for 2027, including capital gains. After subtracting the $33,200 standard deduction, their taxable income would be $96,800, which falls below the 0% threshold.

However, taxable income should include mutual fund distributions, which can "dramatically alter year-end planning projections" and increase taxable income, according to CFP Jim Guarino, managing director at Baker Newman Noyes in Woburn, Massachusetts. He is also a certified public accountant.

If your federal taxable income is above the 0% threshold, you'll pay 15% on the portion of investment gains that exceed the 0% limit, up to that bracket's cap. Gains above that may be taxed at 20%.

Also, the 0% capital gains bracket applies to federal taxes, but your profits could still be subject to state-level taxes, experts say.

As income limits rise for the 0% capital gains bracket due to IRS inflation adjustments, more investors could have tax savings opportunities, experts say.

"There is tons of planning to be done here," especially for early retirees with lower income, according to CFP Dinon Hughes, a partner with Nvest Financial in Portsmouth, New Hampshire.

One strategy, known as "tax gain harvesting," is selling profitable brokerage account assets during lower-income years to leverage the 0% bracket, he said. Keep in mind, these sales stack on top of your other earnings, which could bump taxable income above the 0% threshold.

You can also sell the asset and immediately rebuy it to "reset the cost basis," or original purchase price, said CFP Charles Sachs, chief investment officer of Imperio Wealth Advisors in Coral Gables, Florida.

By resetting the cost basis to current market value, you can reduce future capital gains to trim your tax bill.

When selling assets at a loss, the "wash sale rule" blocks tax-loss harvesting when you rebuy a "substantially identical" asset within 30 days before or after the sale. But the same rule doesn't apply when harvesting gains.

Managing capital gains is only one part of yearly tax planning, according to Guarino with Baker Newman Noyes.

Before selling investments, you should know how boosting AGI could impact your broader financial plan, including income phase-outs for various tax breaks, he said.

For example, modified adjusted gross income can impact a range of tax benefits, such as Affordable Care Act health insurance premium subsidies, which can disappear once earnings exceed the federal limits by even a single dollar.

Another example is President Donald Trump's temporary $6,000 senior "bonus" deduction, which is worth up to $12,000 for married couples per year through 2028.

#2895. Stats Rundown: 4 numbers to know from the Mavericks’ 125-122 comeback win over the Pacers

The Dallas Mavericks (7-4) were on the second night of a back-to-back when they welcomed the Indiana Pacers (3-8) Monday night. They found themselves battling back from a deficit for most of the first half, but in the third quarter they started to find a groove and ultimately pulled away for a 125-122 win in a game that came down to the final possession. Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving led the way, while players like Walter Clayton, Santi Aldama and Caleb Martin did the little things around the edges for what proved to be a total team victory.

The duo of Flagg and Irving is absolutely terrifying when they are "on" and they were on Monday night. The pair dropped 78 points combined on impressive efficiency. Together, they shot 27-of-43, good for a 62.7% connection rate. Irving hit an insane 7-of-10 from downtown, with Flagg an excellent 3-of-6 in his own right. They were also 14-of-15 from the free throw line. Each player individually was a sight to behold, but the combination of what they were doing together was truly next level.

A single game plus/minus needs to be looked at carefully, as it can be misleading. Having said that, Irving played 38 minutes and was a game-high +29 with no other player on either team being even close (the next best was +15 by Daniel Gafford and Andrew Nembhard). Irving's presence was apparent from his scoring, but he did so much more than that as a poised floor general that helped the Mavs to victory in other ways as well.

Don't look now, but Dallas once again dominated on the boards. Being +16 on the glass in a three-point game is unquestionably a big factor in why the Mavs came out on top. The best part of the disparity is that Gafford was in foul trouble most of the night and Morez Johnson, Jr. sat out altogether. Within the overall discrepancy was Dallas' 10-1 offensive rebound advantage.

On the final possession with the Mavericks up by three points, the Pacers were inbounding from half-court. Dusty May substituted Irving for Martin for his length and defensive prowess and Martin rewarded him and Mavs nation with the defensive stop of the night. On a somewhat errant pass across nearly the entire court sideline-to-sideline, Martin streaked in and tipped the ball away from Pascal Siakam, allowing the clock to run out. Pacers' coach Rick Carlisle was furious there was no foul call, however it appeared to be the correct no-call by the referees. Martin got his hand on the ball and tipped it well away from Siakam before the two players' body's made contact with each other. As a result, the Pacers weren't able to attempt a final shot and Dallas got the win.

#2892. Trump's 2028 successors are already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout

Republicans are still reckoning with a historic midterm wipeout, but the fight to assign blame and inherit President Donald Trump's political movement is already underway.

Vice President JD Vance faults the war in Iran. Secretary of State Marco Rubio defends it. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis says Republicans fought the wrong battles. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, argues the party lost touch with voters' economic struggles.

The competing visions from potential presidential contenders offer an early glimpse of the Republican infighting ahead of 2028. But all face the same dilemma: How to convince voters the party can change course without alienating Trump or the MAGA base they need to win the nomination.

The biggest obstacle may be Trump himself, who has shown little appetite for a political retreat.

On Monday, Trump made a surprise appearance in the White House briefing room, declaring the Iran war "militarily is effectively over" while maintaining that the U.S. remains prepared to resume strikes. Earlier that day, he questioned the legitimacy of Republicans' midterm defeat, suggesting without evidence that voting machines were responsible, days after saying that after years of election denial, he would accept the 2026 results.

Since the election, Trump has also replaced Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller and backed Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters against a challenger demanding an accounting of the party's losses.

Trump is also keeping his would-be successors guessing. In a CBS interview Sunday, he praised Rubio alongside Vance but suggested he might stay out of the 2028 Republican primary.

"Maybe I'm better off not getting involved," he said, while emphasizing the weight his endorsement could carry.

That dynamic leaves Vance in a precarious position. Entering the midterms as the clear political heir, Vance now faces a critical question: Can he inherit MAGA without inheriting the blame for Trump's presidency?

In a lengthy post on X Wednesday as election results were still trickling in, Vance challenged Trump's initial explanation for the Republican defeat.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote, arguing voters who backed the Trump-Vance ticket in 2024 abandoned Republicans in 2026 over Iran.

Pointing to foreign policy allows Vance to criticize a defining administration decision without repudiating the broader MAGA movement, while echoing his longstanding opposition to foreign interventions. Vance also has national name recognition and donor ties to help his prospective candidacy.

But the election results complicate Vance's argument.

Just 34% of House voters called the war crucial to their vote, versus 49% citing the cost of living and 55% government corruption, according to the CNBC Voter Poll – suggesting a broader backlash against the Trump administration that Vance has spent nearly two years defending.

"You can't campaign against a war from within an administration you serve," conservative commentator Joel Pollak wrote on X, questioning how Vance could distance himself from a conflict he had publicly defended.

In his CBS interview, Trump said he did not disagree with Vance's assessment and acknowledged the vice president had discussed the post with him beforehand. But he insisted the decision to attack Iran was right and suggested Vance also has losses of his own to explain.

After Vance spent months fundraising and campaigning as Republican National Committee finance chairman, Democrats won both marquee races in his home state of Ohio. Amy Acton defeated Vance ally Vivek Ramaswamy for governor, after the vice president defended a controversial ad featuring Acton's estranged mother. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown claimed Vance's former Senate seat, defeating incumbent Republican Jon Husted.

Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., stated Sunday he would not support Vance in 2028 due to his war criticism, calling it a betrayal of Trump. "You have to be loyal to those people who brought you to the dance," Fine said in an interview with LiveNOW from FOX on Sunday, naming Rubio and Cruz as alternatives.

Rubio is making a different bet: Defend the Iran war while distancing himself from the Republican defeat.

"Sometimes, when you do the right thing, you don't know whether it's popular or not, but it's still the right thing to do," Rubio told reporters Sunday before departing for France.

Rubio, who has denied he plans to run in 2028, largely avoided the campaign trail and has stayed out of the immediate blame game. But his dual role as secretary of state and national security advisor ties him directly to Trump's foreign policy record, which could face renewed scrutiny when Democrats take control of the House. The House may vote this week on articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a rebuke of the Trump administration's foreign policy.

DeSantis, who is not in the Trump administration, is questioning the party's entire playbook.

The outgoing Florida governor called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event" for Republicans at a news conference Wednesday in Tallahassee, Florida, accusing Washington of failing to deliver on its promises while fighting culture wars that no longer resonated with voters.

"Republicans ... really were fighting yesterday's battle," DeSantis said at the news conference.

It was a striking critique from a governor who built his national profile on those same fights.

DeSantis can point to Republicans' ability to retain control of Florida even as Democrats flipped longtime GOP strongholds elsewhere. But Republican Byron Donalds won the governor's race by just 1.3 points, while Democrats gained ground in the Legislature.

Still, Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., credited DeSantis with building a "massive sea wall against the blue tsunami" in an X post.

The scramble to succeed Trump extends well beyond Vance, Rubio and DeSantis.

Cruz called the midterms a "Watergate-level repudiation" in a post on X Wednesday, blaming Trump's tariffs and the prolonged Iran war. Other potential 2028 contenders include Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders and former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, who face the same challenge of moving beyond Trump without alienating his base.

Some wealthy Republican donors are already looking beyond Vance, weighing DeSantis and other alternatives amid concerns that a candidate from Trump's administration would inherit the political baggage of his second term and low voter approval ratings.

The divisions extend to Trump's own coalition. Among voters who backed Republican House candidates, roughly two-thirds of those under 30 approved of Trump's performance, much less than the nearly nine in 10 voters 65 and older, according to the CNBC Voter Poll. Younger Republicans were also more skeptical of the Iran war and U.S. support for Israel, according to the exit poll data.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," Vance said Wednesday. "Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost."

#2891. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac rally as Ackman presses for conservatorship exit

The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to billionaire investor Bill Ackman.

Investors may agree with him, if the rally in both stocks is any sign.

The Federal National Mortgage Association, known as Fannie Mae, and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, have each jumped more than 60% from Oct. 14 to Monday's close. The stocks were both up roughly 3% on Tuesday.

Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, has long pushed for the two entities to be released from federal conservatorship.

"The reason why it's not being touched right now is, you know, midterms," he said in an interview with CNBC's "Squawk Box."

Ackman, who owns both names through Pershing Square, believes Freddie and Fannie have the potential to increase "10-fold from current share prices," he said in his quarterly letter to shareholders, issued on Monday.

Fannie and Freddie buy mortgages from banks and other lenders, and then package them into mortgage-backed securities, known as MBS. Their operations are critical to the housing market, providing liquidity to banks and creating a secondary market for MBS.

The entities were placed into conservatorship in September 2008, during the financial crisis. The stocks were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010 and have traded over the counter since then.

Ackman wants the conservatorship to end, arguing the entities would be worth multiples of their current valuation if they were freed from government control.

President Donald Trump has supported ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie. But it remains politically and economically contentious.

The entities operate under strict capital threshold requirements and would need to be recapitalized, which could happen through issuing common equity. However, the Treasury Department would need to figure out an exit plan for its roughly $388 billion ownership stake in the entities through preferred securities and warrants.

Congress may also need to play a role, passing legislation to restructure the government's role in mortgage financing and home-loan guarantees.

Nonetheless, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently said it could happen before Trump's term ends, telling 2Way's "The Morning Meeting" podcast that the administration will tackle the ownership structure "next year, the year after." He said affordability will be guiding the decision.

One point of controversy is whether ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie would increase the spreads on MBS over Treasuries, effectively making mortgages costlier. Bessent has sought to reassure the market that wouldn't happen.

"Whatever we do is going to be guided by making sure that the spread on [agency] mortgages … over the Treasury does not increase," Bessent said.

Ackman argues that privatizing the GSEs would help insulate them from political meddling. "Fannie and Freddie are these massive, enormously profitable institutions where whichever political party controls them…if they're still in conservatorship, can influence the outcome of elections," he told CNBC.

In one scenario, he explained, Democrats win the White House, conservatorship is still in place, and Democrats push Fannie and Freddie to lower credit standards in order to expand home ownership and affordability.

"If they're going to move more aggressively into borrowers with lower credit quality, for example, to achieve a political objective, that's going to have an impact on trillions of dollars outstanding mortgage securities," Ackman said. "It's going to have an impact on overall credit spreads."

MBS investors want certainty about how the entities will be run, he noted.

"That only gets resolved in a world in which they exit conservatorship, they become publicly traded companies that are owned by institutional and retail investors," Ackman said. "We set the rules. In conservatorship, the president can do anything."

#2890. Game Preview: Knicks vs. Bucks, November 10, 2026

Originally, the Milwaukee Bucks weren't even supposed to be the Milwaukee Bucks. "Robins" was the most popular suggestion in a statewide naming contest in 1968, but somehow the judges weren't so sure about the less-than-fierce image of the little birds with their distinct orange-red breasts. So they opted for "Bucks," a name that honored Wisconsin's antlered-state animal, the white-tailed deer. Contest winner R.D. Trebilcox, who was awarded a brand-new AMC Javelin for his efforts, suggested the name because the animals are "spirited, good jumpers, fast and agile."

Well, going by this year's outfit, the front office might want to think about another contest.

You certainly wouldn't blame any adult male deer for being upset about any sort of connection to Milwaukee's basketball team these days. The current Bucks are hardly spirited, fast, agile, or, frankly, good at doing many things on a basketball court. At 1–9, they're tied with Utah and Sacramento for the worst record in the NBA. During their current six-game losing streak, the Bucks have been outscored by 15.7 points per game. Autsch!

New head coach Taylor Jenkins might already miss the days of coaching consummate professionals like Ja Morant in Memphis, but he should have expected these kinds of growing pains. Everybody and their grandmother knew that the start of the post-Giannis era would be painful in Milwaukee and that it would take time to rebuild a team bereft of picks, outlandish young talent, and meaningful numbers of serious basketball players.

Yes, the Bucks trot out a few solid names like Tyler Herro (21.4 points per game) and Jaime Jaquez Jr. (15.2 points, over 42 percent from three). In theory, they also have some nice young pieces in rookies Brayden Burries (10.5 points) and Nate Ament (over 40 percent from three), along with former Heat hoopers Kel'el Ware and Kasparas Jakučionis. But that's already where the Buck stops (no pun intended), unless you want to count what's left of Kyle Kuzma's and Myles Turner's careers as promising. In reality both of them, and probably a few others, have their agent on speed dial these days, hoping for a trade out of Wisconsin sooner rather than later (see the video of an obviously overweight Turner below).

The rebuilding reality is showing itself in some pretty awful numbers for the Bucks early on. Their offensive rating ranks 27th in the league, and their defensive rating ranks even worse at 28th. One thing they do plenty of is jack up triples (second most in the NBA). The only problem is they hit about a third of them. They play fairly fast, too, with the sixth-highest pace in the league. In the end, though, little in their statistical profile suggests that they actually know what they're doing. Which, of course, is fine for a team this early in a full-blown rebuild.

What does all that misery mean for the Knicks tonight? It means they'll have to concentrate on themselves and make sure the focus is on realizing their own potential, both in this contest and going forward. The world champions have looked a lot better lately as Jalen Brunson has rounded into form (32 points per game and 8 of 17 from three in his last two games) and their outside shooting has gotten less streaky (37.5 percent over the last three). Karl-Anthony Towns has been an Everest-sized rock so far this season, and most of the backups have conducted themselves fairly well in their minutes.

How many minutes some of those reserves see against Milwaukee will likely depend on the availability of Josh Hart, who missed Saturday's game with right ankle soreness. A roster battle is brewing at backup point guard, with Tyler Kolek making the most of his opportunity while Jose Alvarado was briefly out with an injury last week. It'll be interesting to see how this plays out over the next few games and, frankly, over the rest of the season.

Looking over at the Bucks, it's certainly a good problem to have. Milwaukee enjoyed some really good teams over the last decade and change and even has a mesmerizing championship to show for it. That makes the current state of the franchise at least somewhat bearable for the fans, I hope. We all know what hopelessness feels like in the NBA. But as bad as everything looks right now, better times will come. They'll get their young stars to cheer for, and they'll get a system in place that's fun to watch.

And they might even be "spirited, good jumpers, fast and agile" again, just like Bucks are supposed to be.

Who: New York Knicks (5-4) vs. Milwaukee Bucks (1-9)Date: Tuesday, November 10, 2026Time: 7:30 PM ETPlace: Madison Square Garden, New York, NYTV: MSGFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

The Baltimore Ravens have reached a point in the season where changes may be coming. After a difficult stretch, head coach Jesse Minter and his staff have taken more time to evaluate what needs to improve, including personnel, playing time, and the team's overall identity. The evaluation comes as the Ravens prepare to face the Los Angeles Chargers on Monday night. Minter hasn't announced lineup changes, but his message leaves little room for assuming the current approach is sufficient. Baltimore needs its identity to show up in its execution, discipline, and consistency across all three phases.

Minter made it clear that the focus isn't simply on making changes for the sake of making changes. It's about figuring out what the Ravens need to do better and making sure the team plays with a consistent identity.

When asked about the team's self-evaluation during the extra time away from the field, Minter explained what he and his staff have been looking at.

"I appreciate you guys being here. We were able to take advantage of the extra time [of] really looking at ourselves in a self-analysis, self-scout mentality over the last few days. What can I do better? What can we do better as coaches? What can we do better as players? Then, when it comes to scheme, who we're asking to do what, playing time, who do we have in the lineup – I mean, kind of everything, I would say. And now as the guys come back tomorrow, we'll give a little bit of a reset to where we're at with the guys tomorrow. We'll be in a race to improve this week."

The Ravens have struggled to put together consistent performances, and Minter knows the team needs to establish an identity that shows up when it matters most.

When asked whether fans should expect significant lineup or schematic changes following the reset, Minter emphasized the importance of making sure the team's identity matches what the coaching staff expects.

"I think that's for our team. But, I definitely feel like a couple days gives you a chance to really look and really dig deep. I think first and foremost, making sure that the identity that we talk about that we want is not just talk. Sometimes that can get lost as you're racing each week to try to get a game plan in and do things. I'm excited for us to sort of re-establish our identity. [With] lineup changes, I think those are all [on an] individual basis. But there's certain things that we have to have really high standards for. So, we'll see how it all shakes out."

Minter isn't promising wholesale changes, but the message is clear. The Ravens have to be better, and the extra time gives the coaching staff a chance to evaluate what went wrong. Now it's about putting those changes into action and finding a way to get the team back on track.

#2888. FDA warns of vision loss risk linked to popular GLP-1 drugs like Wegovy, Zepbound

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is requiring new safety warnings on all GLP-1 drugs after finding evidence of a potential increased risk of a rare eye condition, the agency said on Monday.

The condition, which can cause sudden vision loss, known as nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), is rare, and a causal relationship has not been established.

The FDA is requiring the makers of all GLP-1 medications to add a warning about the potential increased risk of NAION associated with use of these medications, it said.

NAION is a condition that can result in sudden decreased vision, including permanent vision loss. It is caused by decreased blood flow to the front part of the ​optic nerve — the underlying cause is not completely understood, however.

NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 products, the FDA said.

Ozempic and Wegovy maker Novo Nordisk said it "continues to believe the data do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship, and we remain confident in the benefit-risk profile of our GLP-1 medicines."

CNBC has reached out to Eli Lilly, the company behind Mounjaro, Zepbound and Foundayo, for comment.

The FDA decision follows a review of clinical trials, real-world patient data, and published studies.

An analysis of 126 trials involving more than 134,000 patients found 6.4 cases of NAION per 100,000 patient-years among GLP-1 users, compared with 3.8 among patients receiving other treatments or placebos.

Several observational studies also identified an increased risk, supporting the FDA's concerns.

The FDA's class-wide labeling action is "likely to attract attention but should have limited impact on GLP-1 uptake," according to Citi analysts.

It may temporarily increase patient and investor concern, but the rarity of NAION and substantial weight, glycemic, cardiovascular, renal, and sleep apnea benefits should preserve a favorable benefit-risk profile and limit changes to prescribing the medicines, they added.

While GLP-1 drugs have been shown to lead to benefits beyond weight loss and controlling blood sugar levels, many also carry the FDA's strongest safety warning, known as a boxed warning, over a potential risk of thyroid tumors.

Studies have shown that semaglutide, the active ingredient in Wegovy and Ozempic, and tirzepatide, the active ingredient in Mounjaro, cause thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents. It remains unknown whether the drugs cause these tumors, including a rare form of thyroid cancer, in humans.

#2886. China panel chair Moolenaar demands answers on Nvidia CEO's alleged affair with a Chinese spy

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., said on a Tuesday appearance on CNBC's "Squawk Box" that Congress needs to "get to the bottom" of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Moolenaar, who chairs the House Permanent Select Committee on China, said he wants to know whether Huang shared privileged information with a Chinese spy; whether Huang was influenced to lobby against preventing chip sales to China; and whether China was given preference in purchasing Nvidia's limited supply of advanced chips.

And he urged a thorough internal investigation of Huang.

"If it becomes less of an investigation, more of damage control, that's not going to work because people have to have confidence," Moolenaar said.

"We're dealing with the country, the Chinese Communist Party that is a foremost adversary, that's funding wars and supporting Russia, supporting Iran, North Korea," he said. "And we have basically a Cold War race with technology. We cannot allow the premier company at the forefront of this to, in some way, be irresponsible."

Congressional scrutiny of Huang's affair has intensified since members returned to Washington on Monday.

The New York Times reported that Huang was romantically involved with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive who U.S. intelligence agencies have identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia opened an investigation into its CEO on Sunday. The two Huangs are not related.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said in a press conference on Monday that "we're going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened and what the implications are in terms of national security"

Moolenaar co-authored a letter with Florida Rep. Brian Mast and Arkansas Rep. Rick Crawford on Nov. 5 asking Huang to appear before the Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and House Select Committee on Intelligence. Mast chairs the foreign affairs panel, and Crawford chairs intelligence.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the three Republicans wrote.

#2883. We asked, you answered: Ravens should sell at deadline

The Baltimore Ravens have been buyers so far this season, acquiring center Cam Jurgens from the Philadelphia Eagles in October and quarterback Jacoby Brissett from the Arizona Cardinals last week.

The 4-5 squad now has a 7.5-win over/under and +560 odds to make the playoffs (via FanDuel Sportsbook). 87% of fans think general manager Eric DeCosta should sell before Tuesday's trade deadline, according to last week's SB Nation Reacts survey, including a 57% majority who think an aggressive sale is warranted.

Is he going to be worth a high-end contract in a cornerback market that has exploded in the last year?

His fifth-year option is currently projected to be an affordable $14.25 million (via OverTheCap), making him an attractive short- and long-term addition to another team's secondary. Teams are always more desperate around the deadline, especially for one of the NFL's most important and often-injured positions.

#2882. 'Markets bottom on bad news' maxim rings true as chip stocks rally amid Nvidia scandal

"Markets bottom on bad news," is one of those smart-sounding rules of thumb that proves true just often enough to remain a Wall Street cliché in good standing.

Did the brutal weeks-long punishment of AI stocks culminate last week and reverse higher Monday after a pileup of adverse headlines? In the past week, American voters resoundingly opposed data-center construction across much of the country and Anthropic lowered its target IPO valuation just before a sex-and-espionage scandal struck the one-man embodiment of the entire AI economy, Nvidia's Jensen Huang.

The story of a market taking a cue from a crescendo of bad news after a nasty setback to stage a resounding bounce holds together well enough for now, after Monday's 3.4% jump in the Nasdaq-100 and 7% rip in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX), even as Nvidia shed 4.3%.

Based purely on the tactical evidence, the tech-hardware complex came into the week pretty well washed out and primed to bounce. Numerous trading desks reported historically rare intensity of net selling in the group by institutions into last Thursday's risk purge. The Nasdaq-100 was as oversold on several metrics as it had been at the March 30 Iran-selloff low. The CBOE S&P 500 Volatility Index has put in a nice spike of the sort usually associated with a passing storm, shooting up to 28 and then receding below 20.

The recent dump in the Nasdaq and uptick in risk aversion, "had many elements of capitulation," says Laurent Laskowski, options strategist at Baird Strategas: "record options activity, a sharp spike in volatility, skew and correlations, an inverted VIX curve, and forced liquidations…The setup, therefore, is one where the market is seeing the [downside] left tail narrowing while the [upside] right tail is fattening."

Several technical-analysis gurus (including Macro Risk Advisors' John Kolovos, whose work is cited below) argue the market hasn't quite served up a "fat pitch" to buy the pullback aggressively. Maybe so. But FanGraphs calculates that in Major League Baseball only about 7% of all pitches are in the very center of the strike zone. While those fat pitches result in some 23% of all home runs hit, the other three-quarters of balls that fly over the wall come with less-perfect setups around the edges of the zone.

I wouldn't argue too strenuously against this tech-centered rally carrying on for a bit, for these reasons as well as the fact that valuations have become far less demanding. Last week, I noted Big Tech had not to that point responded to moderately stressed conditions but was getting closer, and "the bull market built on the AI story will almost surely need the AI story to get back on track to keep advancing. A prolonged period when the equal-weight S&P 500 outperforms the market-cap-weighted version is otherwise known – usually – as a bear market." Monday's blip higher could be a start, with plenty still to prove.

But this AI-driven part of the market has lately shown itself less worthy of investor trust, leaving enough hints of structural damage to the bull case that faith can't be restored right away.

In a late-June column, I asked, "Was May 14 a consequential moment for this market, at least tactically?" That date, nearly six months ago, was when the S&P 500 spurted higher to reach the 7500 level for the first time; the index has never reached escape velocity since and in fact crossed above 7500 again just yesterday.

May 14 was when highly touted AI-chip upstart Cerebras came public and its shares more than doubled to a high of $386, as President Trump and China's leader were reported to have made progress on ending the Iran war. Since then, Cerebras has collapsed to $97, the semiconductor group is off 17% and the Iran conflict continues.

A month later the SpaceX IPO was another apparent culmination of New Era tech enthusiasm; it might not have been an important peak in AI excitement, but if it were the market action since would possibly resemble what we've seen since.

Perhaps a half-year reckoning period during which the market has refused to pay up for 30% annual earnings growth for two straight quarters is enough to build a new base constructed on more modest expectations. I've been focused on late-cycle tremors unsettling markets in the form of peak earnings growth, peak capex, peak index concentration, a tighter Federal Reserve and credit flareups. This all explains the market's multi-month stall, and they remain.

But it's important to remain open to the chance that these could end up amounting to mere mid-cycle turbulence, as Morgan Stanley chief investment officer Mike Wilson has been arguing.

First, though, the tape will need to show more progress than a nice, broad single-day comeback. Another rule of thumb holds that a rebound rally needs at least to carry above the 20-day moving average to prove that it's not merely a reflexive dead-cat bounce. This would require a 1.3% gain from Monday's close for the S&P 500, 3.7% for the Nasdaq-100 and 9% for the SOX.

Without pretending any clear sense of what the various Nvidia investigations will mean for its China sales, leadership or long-term earnings power, we can say for sure that the scandal arrived at a fairly opportune time for the market.

Valuations have been pounded to multi-year lows on persistent worry that current profits are unsustainable and the group remains vulnerable to any slowdown in data-center builds. This allowed, for a day, every other semiconductor stock to whistle higher as Nvidia lost some $200 billion in market cap on a blistering $80 billion in dollar-volume traded in the stock.

The S&P 500 as a whole, of course, has grown optically cheaper, too, with semis bolstering the projected earnings and investors declining to give the group credit for their sustainability.

The issue remains that less of those earnings are set to manifest as free cash flow as the hyperscalers spend manically. As this chart comparing the valuation gauges shows, the market looks a good deal less cheap on free cash flow than earnings.

A proper bull case for the market from here might be that the likes of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft will resume harvesting free cash flow, on which investors might place a higher multiple than they're willing to bestow on those hot but hard-to-trust chip makers. Not yet a provable argument.

John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "While sentiment is dire, our concern is that technology is in a 'bad oversold' condition, where seductive bounces fail to produce lasting lows. Instead, the broader equity market may need to follow technology lower, with a more widespread capitulation ultimately needed to wash out weak hands and establish a durable bottom."

-This enjoyable and illuminating review in the New Yorker of James Gleick's "The Telephone: A New History" inevitably summons parallels between the advent of telecommunications and the current AI buildout. Huge privately financed infrastructure buildout, destabilizing new habits of interaction with technology and constant calls for government regulation in exchange for near-monopoly power. The book cites an AT&T ad from 1909 calling telephones "tools of 'civilization . . . one of the most powerful influences for broadening human intelligence.'"

-Moody's Analytics economist Mark Zandi has a helpful thread suggesting AI is so far adding more jobs than it's costing the U.S. economy. The main reasons are sobering though, with most gains coming from data-center construction and wealth creation for those who own AI-dependent stocks. Cold comfort for information-economy job seekers.

-Last week's election triggering a Democratic takeover of Congress brought comparisons to the 1994 "Contract with America" Republican sweep for its magnitude and message. That election, in Bill Clinton's first term, highlighted deep societal fissures and economic instability.

With hindsight, many view the '90s as a placid era of consensus and prosperity, but between the '94 backlash election, constant corporate downsizing, scare-mongering over Federal debt levels, the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing and discomfort with technological change, that decade hit many of today's narrative beats. This Chicago Fed paper, "The decline of job security in the 1990s: Displacement, anxiety, and their effect on wage growth" can fill in some blanks for those not around for it.

Happy fifth anniversary to the peak of a pandemic speculative-tech bull market. Not quite two months before the S&P 500 hit a top in January 2022 as the Fed prepared to choke off surging inflation, perhaps by causing a recession, several key retail-trader-driven subsectors peaked.

The third week of November 2021 was the relative-performance peak in Tesla, as well as the absolute top in Coinbase and the Wisdom Tree Cloud Computing ETF (WCLD).

The five-year lookback period is one of the few time spans shy of 25 years over which the Nasdaq Composite has not outperformed the S&P 500. It's a plus that the broad market can withstand such internal speculative blowoffs, though also a good reminder that the most fun pockets of the market don't stay that way forever.
